terms.definition: The formless base of all matter in alchemy. Everything begins as and can be reduced to this primordial substance—chaos before creation.
The first stage of the alchemical work—blackening, putrefaction, death. Jung interpreted it as confronting the shadow self.
The second stage—whitening, purification, washing away impurities. Psychologically, the emergence of insight from darkness.
The final stage—reddening, the achievement of the philosopher's stone. Symbolizes wholeness, integration, spiritual gold.
The 'Great Work'—the alchemical process of creating the philosopher's stone. Now means any artist's or thinker's masterpiece.
A serpent eating its own tail, symbolizing eternal cyclic renewal. What begins ends where it started—destruction feeding creation.
'Dissolve and coagulate'—the essential alchemical operation. Break down to build up. Destruction precedes creation.
The universal solvent sought by alchemists. Also the life-force or Mercury. The alpha and omega combined.
The alchemical furnace, designed to maintain constant heat. From Arabic for 'oven'. The alchemist's womb.
terms.etymology: Arabic al-tannur (oven)

terms.definition: Heating a substance until reduced to powder or ash. The first operation. Burning away what is not essential.
Dissolving the calcined matter in water or acid. The second operation. What was solid becomes fluid.
Isolating the components of dissolution. The third operation. Sorting what is pure from what is waste.
Recombining the purified elements. The fourth operation. The chemical marriage.
Introduction of new life into the conjunction. The fifth operation. The substance begins to live.
Boiling and condensing to purify. The sixth operation. Rising and falling, ever more refined.
The final solidification of the purified matter. The seventh operation. The stone achieved.
The yellowing stage, sometimes placed between albedo and rubedo. The dawn before full illumination.
The 'peacock's tail'—a display of iridescent colors signaling transition in the work. Beauty mid-transformation.
Not common mercury but the volatile, spiritual principle in all matter. The soul that transforms.
The fixed, fiery principle. Soul as opposed to Mercury's spirit. What gives matter its individuality.
The third principle—body, materiality, the crystallizing force. What makes things solid.
The hermaphroditic figure representing the union of opposites. From 'res bina' (double thing). Completion in duality.
An acronym: 'Visita Interiora Terrae Rectificando Invenies Occultum Lapidem'—Visit the interior of the earth; by rectifying you will find the hidden stone.
The alchemical method of separating and recombining. From Greek 'to tear apart' and 'to gather'. Analysis and synthesis.
terms.etymology: Greek spao (tear) + ageiro (gather)

terms.definition: An essence capable of transmuting base metals. Also a spiritual quality that transforms what it touches.
A liquid form of the philosopher's stone, capable of healing and prolonging life. From Arabic 'al-iksir'.
terms.etymology: Arabic al-iksir

terms.definition: The fifth essence—beyond earth, water, fire, air. The pure, unchanging substance of heavenly bodies.
Increasing the quantity or potency of the philosopher's stone. The stone can make more of itself.
An airtight closure preventing escape of volatile spirits. Named for Hermes. Now 'hermetically sealed'.
A gourd-shaped vessel for distillation—the lower part that holds the liquid. From Latin for gourd.
The still's cap that collects and directs vapor. From Arabic 'al-anbiq'. The distillation apparatus.
terms.etymology: Arabic al-anbiq

terms.definition: A vessel with a long bent neck for distillation. The alchemist's curved thinking.
A circulatory vessel with tubes returning distillate to the body. Named for the bird that feeds its young from its breast.
Maria the Jewess—legendary founder of Western alchemy. Invented the bain-marie, tribikos, and kerotakis.
Thrice-great Hermes—mythical author of the Hermetic texts. Fusion of Greek Hermes and Egyptian Thoth.
The foundational alchemical text, attributed to Hermes. 'As above, so below.' The microcosm mirrors the macrocosm.
The philosopher's stone. Goal of the great work. Transmutes lead to gold, grants immortality, perfects the soul.
The transmutation of base metals into gold. From Greek 'gold-making'. The alchemist's most famous aim.
Drinkable gold—a liquid medicine containing gold. Believed to cure all ailments and extend life.
A beam anchored at only one end, projecting into space — Fallingwater's terraces, diving boards, balconies. The structural drama of defying gravity. Engineering as spectacle.
The arrangement of windows in a building — from Latin fenestra (window). The pattern that gives a façade rhythm. How light enters, how buildings breathe. The eyes of architecture.
The architectural style of raw concrete — béton brut. Le Corbusier's Unité d'Habitation, Boston City Hall. Loved by architects, loathed by the public, rediscovered by Instagram. Honesty as aesthetic.
terms.etymology: From French béton brut (raw concrete)

terms.definition: The German art school (1919-1933) that unified art, craft, and technology — Gropius, Mies, Kandinsky. Form follows function. The template for modernist design. The Nazis closed it; its ideas conquered the world.
terms.etymology: German: Bau (building) + Haus (house)

terms.definition: Columns that raise a building above ground — Le Corbusier's Five Points of Architecture. The building floats; the ground flows beneath. Freeing the plan from the earth.
A structural bracket projecting from a wall to support weight — the technique that built Gothic cathedrals and Medieval castles. Stone stepping out to catch stone. The medieval cantilever.
The external arched support that channels Gothic cathedral walls' outward thrust to the ground — engineering that enabled walls of glass. Structure made visible and beautiful.
The central organizing idea of an architectural design — the big move, the diagram, the concept from which all decisions flow. Not the whole solution but its seed.
The solid mass in architectural drawings shown as filled black — walls, structure, the space you can't occupy. The figure-ground relationship. What's not room is poché.
Intense final design sprint — from the cart (charrette) that collected student drawings at the École des Beaux-Arts. Now any deadline crunch. The all-nighter before presentation.
The lowest part of an entablature, resting directly on column capitals. The main beam spanning columns.
The horizontal structure above columns: architrave, frieze, and cornice. The classical crown.
The middle band of an entablature, often decorated with sculpture. The Parthenon's frieze is legendary.
The projecting horizontal molding crowning a building or wall. The final flourish.
The triangular gable end of a roof, especially in classical architecture. Often filled with sculpture.
A row of columns supporting a roof or entablature. The parade of verticals.
A colonnade surrounding a building or courtyard. Greek temples were often peripteral.
A porch with a roof supported by columns, often at a building's entrance.
A sculpted female figure serving as a column. The Erechtheion's maidens bearing the roof.
A sculpted male figure serving as a column. The masculine counterpart to caryatids.
A flat column attached to a wall, projecting slightly. Decorative, not structural.
A column partially embedded in a wall. Half-free, half-bound.
Vertical grooves carved into a column shaft. Creates play of light and shadow.
The subtle swelling of a column's shaft. Corrects the optical illusion of concavity.
The top step of a temple platform on which columns stand.
The foundation platform of a Greek temple, below the stylobate.
The inner chamber of a Greek or Roman temple, housing the cult statue.
The vestibule or porch before a temple's cella.
The rear chamber of a Greek temple, often a treasury.
The oldest and simplest Greek order: sturdy columns, no base, plain capitals. Masculine, severe.
Greek order with slender columns, scroll capitals (volutes), and base. Elegant, feminine.
Greek order with ornate capitals of acanthus leaves. The most decorative.
Roman order: simplified Doric, unfluted columns. Plain, robust.
Roman order combining Ionic volutes with Corinthian acanthus. Maximalist.
The spiral scroll of an Ionic capital. The shell-like curl.
The spiny Mediterranean plant whose leaves ornament Corinthian capitals.
The flat slab atop a column capital, supporting the architrave.
The curved molding below the abacus in Doric capitals. Sea-urchin shaped.
A panel between triglyphs in a Doric frieze, often sculpted.
A grooved block in a Doric frieze, with three vertical channels.
Small rectangular blocks in a row, like teeth, in Ionic/Corinthian cornices.
An ornamental bracket under a cornice, especially Corinthian.
An ornament at the apex or corners of a pediment.
An upright ornament at the eaves, concealing tile ends.
Masonry with deep joints and rough surfaces, creating bold texture. Renaissance power.
Masonry of precisely cut rectangular stones with thin joints.
A wedge-shaped stone forming an arch. The keystone is the central voussoir.
The central wedge-shaped stone at an arch's crown, locking all others in place.
The projecting molding atop a pier or pilaster from which an arch springs.
The triangular space between an arch and its rectangular frame.
The underside of an arch, balcony, or overhanging eave.
An arched ceiling or roof. Barrel, groin, rib, fan—many types evolved.
The simplest vault: a continuous semicircular arch. A tunnel of stone.
Two barrel vaults intersecting at right angles. The groins are the edges.
A vault with visible ribs along the groins. Gothic structural innovation.
English Gothic vault with fan-shaped ribs spreading from springs. King's College Chapel.
A curved triangle transitioning from square base to circular dome. Byzantine solution.
An arch across a corner, bridging square to octagon to dome. Alternative to pendentive.
A hemispherical roof. The Pantheon, Hagia Sophia, St. Peter's—architecture's crown.
A circular opening, especially at a dome's apex. The Pantheon's eye to heaven.
A small turret with windows crowning a dome, admitting light.
A cylindrical wall supporting a dome.
A small dome, especially one atop a larger roof or tower.
A semicircular recess, especially at the east end of a church.
The central aisle of a church, where the congregation sits.
A passage flanking the nave, separated by columns or piers.
The arms of a cross-shaped church, crossing the nave.
Where nave and transept intersect. Often crowned by a tower or dome.
The eastern part of a church around the altar, for clergy.
The part of a church between nave and altar where singers sit.
A walkway around the apse, allowing circulation behind the altar.
The upper level of a church wall with windows above aisle roofs.
A shallow gallery between the arcade and clerestory.
A mass of masonry projecting from a wall to resist outward thrust.
A small ornamental turret, especially atop buttresses. Weight and decoration.
Carved leaf-like ornaments along Gothic spires and pinnacles.
Ornamental stonework in Gothic windows, supporting the glass.
A vertical bar dividing window panes.
A circular window with radiating tracery. Gothic cathedrals' crowning glory.
A tall narrow window with a pointed arch. Early Gothic.
The vestibule at a church's entrance, before the nave.
An open central court, especially in Roman houses. Roofless heart.
The sunken basin in a Roman atrium, catching rainwater.
The opening in a Roman atrium roof above the impluvium.
A colonnaded garden courtyard in a Roman house.
Roman underfloor heating system. Hot air circulating beneath raised floors.
Roman public baths—caldarium, tepidarium, frigidarium.
A Roman public hall with nave and aisles. Later the church plan.
A freestanding arch commemorating victory. Roman emperors' monuments.
An oval arena with tiered seating all around. The Colosseum.
The seating area of a Roman theater or amphitheater.
The circular dancing floor in a Greek theater; semicircular in Roman.
The stage area before the scene building. Later, the arch framing the stage.
The elaborate facade behind a Roman theater stage.
A passage through which crowds enter or exit an amphitheater. 'Spewing' people.
Honeycomb vaulting: tiers of niche-like cells creating a stalactite ceiling. Islamic geometric wonder.
A vaulted hall open on one side. Four iwans often face a courtyard.
A niche in a mosque wall indicating the direction of Mecca.
The pulpit in a mosque from which sermons are delivered.
The tower from which the muezzin calls to prayer.
The direction of Mecca; the qibla wall contains the mihrab.
The central courtyard of a mosque.
A covered arcade around a mosque courtyard.
A projecting oriel window with wooden latticework. Privacy, shade, ventilation.
Moroccan mosaic tilework: hand-cut geometric pieces forming complex patterns.
A monumental portal projecting from a facade, framing an iwan.
Four-garden: Persian garden divided into quadrants by water channels. Paradise geometry.
Persian wind tower: catches breezes and channels cool air into buildings.
An underground aqueduct bringing mountain water to desert cities. Persian engineering.
A roadside inn for caravans: courtyard, stables, rooms for merchants.
A bathhouse in Islamic architecture: hot rooms, domed ceilings, star-shaped skylights.
The tower above the sanctuary of a North Indian Hindu temple. Mountain peak pointing to heaven.
The tower above the sanctuary in South Indian temple architecture.
The monumental gateway tower of a South Indian temple. Teeming with sculpture.
A pillared hall or pavilion in Indian temple architecture.
The 'womb-chamber': the innermost sanctuary of a Hindu temple, housing the deity.
The circumambulatory path around a temple or shrine.
An ornamental gateway, especially at Buddhist stupas.
A Buddhist hemispherical mound containing relics. Sacred architecture of enlightenment.
A Buddhist prayer hall, often rock-cut, with a stupa at the end.
A Buddhist monastery: cells around a courtyard.
A perforated stone or wood screen. Indian mashrabiya. Light filtered, privacy maintained.
An elevated dome-shaped pavilion. 'Umbrella'—decorative or commemorative.
A traditional Indian mansion, often with courtyards and ornate facades.
Indian water architecture: stairs descending to water level. Vav, baoli—cool refuges.
The ribbed disc-like stone atop a shikhara, below the finial.
Chinese bracket system: interlocking wooden blocks supporting roof eaves. Structural poetry.
A narrow lane between traditional Beijing courtyard houses. Urban intimacy.
A Beijing courtyard house: buildings on four sides around a central yard.
A Chinese memorial or ceremonial gateway. Ornate roofed arches.
Chinese pagoda: multi-tiered tower, evolved from Indian stupa. Buddhist architecture.
A Chinese pavilion: open-sided, often in gardens. Rest and contemplation.
A circular doorway in Chinese gardens. Frame and passage.
Chinese geomancy: the art of orienting buildings to harmonize with cosmic forces.
The gateway marking entrance to a Shinto shrine. Sacred threshold.
Japanese study-hall style: tatami, alcove (tokonoma), built-in desk. Zen aesthetic.
A recessed alcove in a Japanese room for displaying art and flowers.
Sliding panels that divide Japanese rooms. Opaque, often painted.
Paper-covered sliding screens admitting diffused light. The soft wall.
A wooden veranda along a Japanese building. Inside-outside threshold.
Traditional Kyoto townhouse: narrow facade, deep interior, courtyard gardens.
Traditional Japanese farmhouse with thatched roof and earthen floor areas.
A Japanese roof style combining hipped and gabled forms.
Dry landscape garden: raked gravel, rocks, no water. Zen minimalism.
Traditional Korean house with curved roof, heated floor (ondol), natural materials.
Korean underfloor heating: flues carry heat from kitchen fire under stone floor.
Traditional Korean decorative painting on wooden buildings: vivid geometric patterns.
Mesoamerican architectural style: sloping wall (talud) topped by vertical panel (tablero). Teotihuacan signature.
Aztec skull rack: wooden structure displaying skulls of sacrificial victims.
A raised Mayan roadway of white limestone. 'White road.'
A natural sinkhole exposing groundwater, sacred to the Maya. Architecture of descent.
A Mayan underground storage chamber carved into bedrock.
A false arch made by stepping stones progressively inward. Mayan vaulting.
Sun-dried mud brick. The material of Saharan architecture, Pueblo buildings.
West African mud-brick coated with mud plaster. The material of Djenné.
A traditional round African dwelling with conical thatched roof.
A Southern African enclosure for livestock, or a village of huts around such a space.
Flowing organic forms, sinuous lines, natural motifs. Gaudí, Horta, Guimard. 1890-1910.
Geometric elegance, bold colors, luxurious materials. Chrysler Building. 1920s-30s.
Modernist architecture: glass, steel, flat roofs, open plans. Mies, Gropius, Le Corbusier.
Sun-break: external shading devices. Le Corbusier's response to glass walls.
A non-structural exterior wall, typically glass. The skyscraper's skin.
Fragmented, distorted forms challenging structural logic. Gehry, Hadid, Libeskind.
Computer-generated organic forms from algorithmic parameters. Zaha Hadid's later work.
1960s Japanese movement: megastructures, capsules, biological metaphors. Kurokawa, Tange.
Celebrating structure and services: exposed pipes, visible framework. Rogers, Foster, Piano.
Modernism adapted to local climate, culture, materials. Against placeless universalism.
Building traditions of ordinary people using local materials and techniques. Before architects.
A Russian country cottage. Summer retreat, potato garden, birch trees, nostalgia.
A traditional Russian log house with decorated window frames.
The bulbous dome of Russian Orthodox churches. St. Basil's rainbow domes.
The icon-covered wall separating nave from sanctuary in Orthodox churches.
A Polish manor house: country seat of the szlachta. Columned portico, wings.
Traditional Ukrainian whitewashed cottage with thatched roof.
Slovenian traditional hayrack. Unique Alpine architecture.
Courtyard: the center of Slavic domestic life.
The treatment of light and shade in drawing and painting; by extension, the interplay of contrasting elements in any art form or situation.
terms.etymology: Chiaro (clear, light) + scuro (dark, obscure)
terms.usage: Caravaggio mastered chiaroscuro to create dramatic psychological intensity.

terms.definition: The technique of softening outlines and transitions — Leonardo's smoky, hazy effect where edges dissolve into atmosphere. The Mona Lisa's smile exists in sfumato: look directly and it vanishes; look away and it appears. Ambiguity as method.
terms.etymology: Italian: sfumare (to evaporate, to shade off)

terms.definition: When earlier painting shows through later layers — the artist's visible change of mind. X-rays reveal hidden compositions beneath finished works. Lillian Hellman's memoir borrowed the term: the past showing through the present. Evidence of revision, of second thoughts.
terms.etymology: Italian: pentirsi (to repent)

terms.definition: Thick, textured application of paint — built up in sculptural layers so brushstrokes and knife marks remain visible. Van Gogh's swirling skies. Rembrandt's jewels. The paint itself becomes subject, not just medium.
terms.etymology: Italian: impastare (to knead, to paste)

terms.definition: Art that deceives the eye into seeing three dimensions in two — painted flies you try to swat, open windows that are walls, architectural spaces that don't exist. From Zeuxis painting grapes birds tried to eat. Illusion as virtuosity.
terms.etymology: French: tromper (to deceive) + l'œil (the eye)

terms.definition: Purification, cleansing — Aristotle's explanation of tragedy's effect: through pity and fear, we purge those emotions. Medical metaphor: drama as therapy. Or intellectual clarification: understanding brings relief. The meaning is still debated; the word stuck.
terms.etymology: Greek: kathairein (to cleanse)

terms.definition: Nesting dolls: a set of wooden figures that open to reveal smaller ones inside.
Russian folk decorative painting: black, red, gold on wood. Floral patterns.
Russian blue-and-white ceramics. Delicate floral patterns on porcelain.
Russian lacquer miniatures: tiny paintings on boxes. Icon painting secularized.
Ukrainian decorated Easter egg. Wax-resist dyeing, geometric patterns.
'Thousand flowers': glass technique using cross-sections of colored glass rods.
Shaping glass with a torch. Beads, figurines, scientific glass.
Glass shaped by inflating molten glass on a blowpipe. Ancient Syrian invention.
Venetian glassmaking tradition. Sequestered on Murano island. Trade secrets.
Clear Venetian glass, approaching crystal clarity. 15th-century innovation.
Glass with embedded white or colored threads in patterns.
Glass with metallic sparkles from copper or chromic oxide.
Layered glass with design carved in relief. Portland Vase.
Crusite glass paste molded and fired. Art Nouveau revival.
Colored glass in lead frames. Cathedral windows. Light transformed.
A thin layer of colored glass over clear, which can be etched through.
Slow cooling to relieve internal stress. Prevents cracking.
A blob of molten glass collected on the blowpipe.
An iron rod for holding glass during shaping. Leaves a 'pontil mark.'
A flat surface for shaping molten glass. Originally marble.
A small furnace opening for reheating glass during working.
Broken or waste glass for recycling into new batches.
Granulated glass, partially fused. Used in glazes and enamel.
Glass with milky, iridescent quality. Tiffany's specialty.
Inlaying gold or silver wire into steel. Named for Damascus.
Shaping metal by hammering from the reverse side. Relief work.
Refining repoussé work by hammering from the front side.
Black metallic alloy inlaid in engraved silver or gold. Dark contrast.
Japanese technique: layered metals forged and manipulated to resemble wood grain.
Enamel filling compartments formed by wire strips soldered to a base.
Enamel filling recesses carved into metal. Limoges work.
Translucent enamel without backing. Stained glass in metal.
Fusing tiny metal spheres to a surface. Etruscan mastery.
Delicate ornamental work of fine wire. Lace in metal.
Cutting lines into metal with a burin. Permanent incision.
Using acid to bite lines into metal through a resist.
Chemical treatment to color metal surfaces. Controlled aging.
Smoothing metal by light hammering. Refining the surface.
Forming a vessel by hammering flat sheet over a stake.
Forming metal over a rotating mandrel. Lathe-based shaping.
Shaping heated metal by hammering. The blacksmith's art.
Rapid cooling of heated metal, hardening it.
Reheating quenched metal to reduce brittleness while keeping hardness.
Setting one material into recesses cut in another. Contrasting surfaces.
Applying one metal over another. Decorative layer.
Japanese copper-gold alloy, patinated to blue-black. Sword fittings.
Japanese copper-silver alloy. Gray, subtle. Sword guards.
Indo-Persian gold or silver inlay on steel. Mughal weapons, armor.
Indian zinc alloy inlaid with silver. From Bidar. Black and silver.
Japanese lacquer from the urushi tree sap. Builds up in dozens of coats.
Japanese lacquer decoration: gold or silver powder sprinkled on wet lacquer.
'Pear skin ground': gold flakes under transparent lacquer. Shimmering.
Mother-of-pearl inlay in lacquer. Iridescent shell fragments.
Red lacquer over black, worn to reveal underlayer. Accidental beauty.
Japanese carved wood lacquerware. Red lacquer over carved patterns.
Chinese carved red lacquer, built up in hundreds of layers then carved.
Chinese incised lacquer filled with color. Named for the Indian coast trade route.
European imitation of Asian lacquer. Varnish and paint, not true lacquer.
A book size from sheets folded twice, making four leaves (eight pages).
A book size from sheets folded three times, making eight leaves.
A book size from sheets folded to make twelve leaves. Also 'twelvemo.'
Fine goatskin leather for binding. Takes gold tooling well.
Calfskin leather for binding. Smooth, takes polish.
Fine animal skin for writing or binding. Finer than parchment.
Animal skin prepared for writing. Sheep or goat.
Impressing designs into leather binding, often with gold leaf.
Tooling without gold—impression only.
Book edges covered with gold leaf.
The decorative band at head and tail of spine.
The paper joining book block to covers. Often decorative.
The endpaper pasted to the inside of the cover.
The free leaf of the endpaper.
Horizontal ridges across the spine from sewing cords.
A cover made separately then attached to the book block.
Gluing pages to a cover at the spine. Paperback standard.
Binding with staples through the fold. Magazines, pamphlets.
Ancient chain-stitch binding allowing book to open flat.
A book of bound pages, as opposed to a scroll. The format we still use.
The front edge of the book, opposite the spine.
Brown spots on old paper from fungus or oxidation.
Decorative paper with swirled patterns from floating pigments.
Lace-like tooled border on fine bindings. French specialty.
The scent trail left behind. 'Wake' in English. How far your perfume travels.
The first scents perceived, evaporating quickly. Citrus, herbs.
The middle of a fragrance, emerging as top notes fade. Florals, spices.
The foundation, lasting longest. Woods, musks, resins.
A blend of notes creating a unified impression. The chord of perfumery.
A fragrance family: bergamot, oakmoss, labdanum. Named for Cyprus.
'Fern': lavender, oakmoss, coumarin. Classic masculine family.
Warm, spicy, resinous fragrances. Vanilla, amber, incense.
Edible scents: vanilla, chocolate, caramel. Sweet and delicious.
Fresh, ozonic, marine scents. A 1990s innovation.
Whale-derived fixative. Rare, valuable, now mostly synthetic.
Highly concentrated plant extract obtained by solvent extraction.
Concentrated plant extract obtained by distillation or pressing.
Extracting fragrance by pressing flowers into fat. Ancient, labor-intensive.
Soaking materials in solvent to extract fragrance.
A substance that slows evaporation, making fragrance last.
Small-batch, artisanal fragrance. Versus designer/mass market.
A perfumer. One who creates fragrances professionally.
How a fragrance smells after it settles. The base notes in action.
Any function beyond basic timekeeping. Calendar, chronograph, repeater.
A rotating cage compensating for gravity's effect on accuracy. Haute horlogerie showpiece.
The mechanism releasing energy in controlled increments. The tick.
The oscillating wheel regulating timekeeping. The heart of a watch.
The coiled spring storing energy. Power source of mechanical watches.
Self-winding: a rotor winds the mainspring with wrist movement.
A specific movement design. Each has a number.
The mechanism inside a watch. Mechanical or quartz.
Synthetic ruby bearings reducing friction. '17 jewels.'
A stopwatch function: measure elapsed time.
A complication tracking date, day, month, leap years.
A complication chiming the time on demand. Audible timekeeping.
A repeater striking hours and quarters automatically. The king of complications.
A complication displaying lunar cycle. Poetic timekeeping.
Indicator showing remaining mainspring energy.
Engine-turned engraving: precise geometric patterns on dials.
Watch face coated with fired enamel. Grand feu technique.
'High watchmaking': the pinnacle of craft. Patek, Vacheron, Audemars.
Unit of gem weight: 200 milligrams. Derived from carob seeds.
The total light reflected from a gem. Internal and external reflection.
Spectral colors dispersed by a gem. Rainbows flashing.
Flashes of light when gem, light source, or viewer moves.
Internal feature: crystal, feather, needle. Flaws or character.
Degree of freedom from inclusions. FL to I3 scale for diamonds.
How a gem is shaped and faceted. Determines light performance.
Round cut with 57 or 58 facets. Maximizes brilliance.
Rectangular facets in steps. Emerald cut, Asscher.
A gem polished but not faceted. Domed, smooth surface.
The bottom portion of a cut gem, below the girdle.
The top portion of a cut gem, above the girdle.
The widest part of a cut gem, where crown meets pavilion.
The flat top facet of a cut gem.
The tiny facet at the bottom point of a cut gem.
A small magnifying lens for examining gems. 10x standard.
No inclusions visible to the naked eye.
Glowing under UV light. Some diamonds fluoresce blue.
Showing different colors from different angles. Tanzanite.
A star effect from light reflecting off needle inclusions. Star sapphire.
Cat's eye effect: a moving line of light. Tiger's eye, chrysoberyl.
Hardness scale 1-10. Diamond is 10, talc is 1.
A choreographed pattern of movements encoding combat techniques. The living textbook of a martial art, passed down through bodies.
The focus of physical and mental energy at the moment of impact. The explosive concentration that makes a technique decisive.
Continued awareness and alertness after a technique. The fight isn't over when you think it is—maintain readiness.
A sharp exhalation or shout focusing energy and spirit at the moment of action. The sound of ki (vital energy) being released.
A training hall for martial arts. Literally 'place of the way'—the physical space where the path is practiced.
Teacher or master. Literally 'one who came before'—someone who walks the path ahead of you and shows the way.
A rank indicating proficiency level, typically starting after achieving black belt. The dan ranks represent deepening mastery.
'Touched': a valid hit. Also acknowledgment of a point in argument.
An attack immediately following a parry. Counter-strike.
Deflecting an attack with the blade. Eight basic parries.
The basic attacking footwork: extending front leg while pushing off back.
A running attack, crossing feet. 'Arrow.'
A short jump forward followed by a lunge.
The fencing strip: 14 meters long, 1.5-2 meters wide.
The ready position. Also the referee's command.
A fencing match between two fencers.
The lightest weapon, point-only, target is torso.
The dueling sword: point-only, entire body is target.
A cutting weapon: point and edge score, target is above waist.
Priority rules in foil and sabre: who has the attack.
The initial offensive action threatening the target.
An offensive action into an opponent's attack.
A fake attack to draw a parry, creating an opening.
Moving the blade around opponent's blade to attack another line.
Striking opponent's blade sharply to create an opening.
Taking opponent's blade diagonally from high to low or vice versa.
Body contact, which halts the action. A fault if intentional.
The point in orbit farthest from the Sun.
The point in orbit closest to the Sun.
The point in orbit farthest from Earth. Also: highest point.
The point in orbit closest to Earth.
The Sun's apparent path through the sky. The zodiac belt.
The point directly overhead. From Arabic 'samt ar-ras.'
The point directly below, opposite the zenith. Lowest point.
Horizontal direction measured in degrees from north.
Angular height above the horizon.
Celestial longitude, measured in hours from the vernal equinox.
Celestial latitude, measured in degrees from the celestial equator.
Measured relative to stars. Sidereal day is 4 minutes shorter than solar.
3.26 light-years. Distance at which 1 AU subtends one arcsecond.
Distance light travels in one year. About 9.5 trillion kilometers.
Earth-Sun distance. About 150 million kilometers.
Brightness measure: lower is brighter. Sirius is -1.46.
The Moon's apparent wobble, revealing 59% of its surface over time.
The line between day and night on a planet or moon.
Three bodies in alignment. Sun-Earth-Moon at new and full moons.
When a planet is opposite the Sun from Earth. Best viewing.
A body passing across the face of a larger one. Mercury transiting the Sun.
One body hiding another. The Moon occults stars.
Apparent backward motion of a planet. An optical illusion of orbits.
Earth's axis slowly wobbles over 26,000 years. The pole star changes.
A small wobble superimposed on precession. 18.6-year cycle.
'The Follower': bright star in Taurus, following the Pleiades.
'Hand of the Giant': red supergiant in Orion's shoulder.
'Foot': blue supergiant in Orion's foot.
'Tail': the tail of Cygnus the Swan. Part of the Summer Triangle.
'Falling Eagle': brightest star in Lyra. Once the pole star, will be again.
'Flying Eagle': brightest star in Aquila.
'Mouth of the Fish': lonely bright star in the southern autumn sky.
Open-air living; a philosophy of spending time outdoors to nurture the soul. Not just outdoor recreation but a way of life connected to nature.
terms.etymology: From fri (free) + luft (air) + liv (life)

terms.definition: A state of warmth, friendliness, and good cheer; cozy belonging. The feeling of a good Gasthaus with old friends.
A cozy, convivial atmosphere; the warmth of being with good people in a pleasant environment. More active and social than hygge.
terms.etymology: From gezel (companion) + -ig + -heid (quality)

terms.definition: A quality of coziness and comfortable conviviality that engenders a feeling of contentment or well-being. The art of creating warmth and intimacy in everyday moments.
terms.etymology: From Old Norse hugga (to comfort, console)

terms.definition: Comfortable, relaxed, at ease; physical and mental well-being. Sabai sabai means taking it easy.
Forest bathing; the practice of immersing oneself in the atmosphere of a forest for restorative benefit. A form of nature therapy.
terms.etymology: From 森林 (shinrin, forest) + 浴 (yoku, bathing)

terms.definition: The perceptual world of an organism — the slice of reality accessible to its senses and relevant to its survival. A tick's Umwelt is warmth, butyric acid, and hair. A bat's is echolocation. Yours is the narrow band of electromagnetic radiation you call visible light. Jakob von Uexküll's concept: every species lives in its own universe.
terms.etymology: German: um (around) + Welt (world)

terms.definition: Programmed cell death — the cell's elegant suicide for the good of the organism. Distinct from necrosis (traumatic death). Your body kills 50-70 billion cells daily. Without apoptosis: cancer. Too much: neurodegeneration. The word was coined to echo the Greek for leaves falling from trees.
terms.etymology: Greek: apo (away) + ptosis (falling)

terms.definition: Cellular self-eating — the recycling system where cells digest their own damaged components. Essential for survival during starvation, for clearing protein aggregates, for longevity. Yoshinori Ohsumi won the 2016 Nobel for working out the machinery. Fasting activates it. Dysfunction causes Parkinson's, Alzheimer's, cancer.
terms.etymology: Greek: auto (self) + phagein (to eat)

terms.definition: The observable characteristics of an organism — the expression of genotype filtered through environment, development, and chance. Your height, your eye color, your susceptibility to addiction. Dawkins extended it: beaver dams are part of beaver phenotype. Genes reach beyond the body.
terms.etymology: Greek: phainein (to show) + typos (type)

terms.definition: When the effect of one gene depends on the presence of other genes — genetic interactions that break the simple one-gene-one-trait model. Explains why identical mutations have different effects in different genetic backgrounds. The genome is a network, not a list.
terms.etymology: Greek: epi (upon) + stasis (standing)

terms.definition: When a single gene affects multiple, seemingly unrelated traits. The sickle cell gene: one copy protects against malaria, two copies cause anemia. Evolution cannot optimize traits independently because genes are tangled together.
terms.etymology: Greek: pleion (more) + tropos (way, turn)

terms.definition: The tendency of living systems to maintain stable internal conditions — temperature, pH, glucose, everything. Claude Bernard's milieu intérieur. Walter Cannon's wisdom of the body. Not equilibrium but dynamic stability: constant adjustment to stay the same.
terms.etymology: Greek: homoios (similar) + stasis (standing still)

terms.definition: Bacterial communication — microbes release signaling molecules and respond when concentration crosses a threshold, indicating sufficient population density. Collective behavior emerging from individual cells counting their neighbors. Biofilms, bioluminescence, virulence: all coordinated this way. Bacteria vote.

In glass — biological processes performed in lab containers rather than living organisms. In vitro fertilization. Contrast with in vivo (in the living). The controlled experiment outside the messy body.
In the living — within a living organism. Drug testing moves from in vitro to in vivo before human trials. The real test, with all biological complexity.
Japanese low-fire ceramic for tea bowls. Removed glowing, cooled rapidly. Wabi-sabi aesthetic.
Pale green glaze, especially Korean. The color of secret jade.
Tin-glazed earthenware, brightly painted. Italian Renaissance. Via Majorca.
Dutch blue-and-white tin-glazed pottery. Imitating Chinese porcelain.
Tin-glazed pottery, named for Faenza, Italy. French term for majolica.
White, translucent ceramic fired at high temperature. China's secret.
Dense, vitrified ceramic between earthenware and porcelain.
Porous ceramic fired at low temperature. The most ancient pottery.
Unglazed fired ceramic. The first firing before glazing.
Liquid clay for coating, decorating, or joining pottery.
Glassy coating fused to ceramic surface. Color, waterproofing, beauty.
Network of fine cracks in glaze. Sometimes a defect, sometimes cultivated.
Forming pottery on a spinning wheel. Centrifugal shaping.
Building pottery by stacking ropes of clay. Ancient technique.
Constructing pottery from flat sheets of clay.
The furnace for firing pottery. From wood-fired to electric.
A protective container for pottery during firing.
Firing with limited oxygen, affecting glaze colors. Copper goes red.
Firing with ample oxygen. Standard kiln atmosphere.
Japanese folk craft movement. Beauty in humble, functional objects.
The porcelain capital of China. Imperial kilns for a millennium.
White Dehua porcelain from Fujian. Figures, vessels, pure white.
Chinese porcelain with pink enamel palette. Qing dynasty.
Decoration applied before glazing and firing. Blue-and-white.
Decoration applied over fired glaze, requiring additional firing.
Scratching through slip to reveal clay beneath. Decorative contrast.
Everything in the frame: set, lighting, costume, actor placement. What's 'put in the scene.'
Editing to create meaning through juxtaposition. Eisenstein's theory.
Sound from within the story world. Characters can hear it.
Sound from outside the story: score, narration. Characters can't hear it.
An abrupt edit within a scene. Godard's disruption.
An edit linking two shots by visual similarity. Bone to spaceship.
A transition where one shot fades into the next.
Gradual transition to or from black (or white).
Camera moving alongside action. On tracks, dolly, or Steadicam.
Camera platform on wheels. Dolly in: move toward subject.
Camera rotating horizontally on its axis.
Camera rotating vertically on its axis.
Camera on a crane, rising or swooping.
Stabilized handheld camera for smooth movement. The Shining's corridors.
Keeping foreground and background in sharp focus. Citizen Kane.
Only one plane in focus, blurring the rest. Directs attention.
Shifting focus from one subject to another within a shot.
The frame's width to height. 4:3 classic TV, 16:9 widescreen, 2.35:1 scope.
Dark 1940s-50s crime films: shadows, cynicism, femmes fatales.
French New Wave: Godard, Truffaut. Breaking rules, personal vision.
Italian postwar cinema: location shooting, non-actors, social themes.
The director as author. Personal vision despite industrial production.
Hitchcock's term: the object everyone wants but doesn't really matter.
Post-production sound effects: footsteps, rustling. Named for Jack Foley.
Automated Dialogue Replacement: re-recording dialogue in studio.
Matching details between shots. Continuity errors break the illusion.
A face in need of a slap; someone whose appearance invites a punch. German precision in describing the punchable.
Beautiful figure; the art of making a good impression. Appearance, style, and dignity combined.
The ring left on a table by a cold glass; the watermark of conviviality.
The study of what lies behind; the Italian art of finding hidden motives and conspiracies behind every event.
The sweetness of doing nothing; pleasant idleness elevated to an art form.
terms.etymology: Dolce (sweet) + far (to do) + niente (nothing)
terms.usage: The Italian concept of dolce far niente stands in contrast to Protestant work ethics.

terms.definition: The Swedish coffee break elevated to cultural institution; taking time to slow down with coffee and pastry.
A woman, often elderly, who cares for stray cats. A specific Italian archetype of urban compassion.
terms.etymology: From gatto (cat)

terms.definition: 'All pull together'; communal self-help and unity. Kenya's national motto—collective effort for common good.
Homeland in the deepest sense; not just birthplace but the landscape, culture, and community that shape one's identity. Where the soul feels at home.
A meeting or conference; important discussion where all voices are heard. Traditional African consensus-building.
Drinking at home alone in your underwear with no intention of going out. Finnish honest self-care.
A state of blissful relaxation; the pleasure of doing nothing in particular while enjoying tea, conversation, or simply being. Turkish dolce far niente.
To scheme, finagle, or work the system; the art of creative problem-solving through unofficial channels, developed under communist-era scarcity.
To rest in the shade at midday; to escape the Mediterranean heat in drowsy contemplation. Made famous by Montale's poetry.
terms.etymology: From meriggio (midday)

terms.definition: 'I see you'; the Zulu greeting that acknowledges someone's full presence and humanity. Response: Ngikhona (I am here).
A schnapps idea; a plan conceived while drunk that seems brilliant but is foolish.
Studied carelessness; the art of performing difficult tasks with such ease that they appear effortless. A Renaissance ideal of aristocratic grace.
terms.etymology: From Italian 'sprezzare' (to disdain)
terms.usage: Castiglione advocated sprezzatura as essential to the perfect courtier.

terms.definition: Harpoon; Greek slang for men who pursue tourists romantically. A summer coastal phenomenon.
'Maybe it'll work out'; blind trust in fate. Reckless optimism without planning.
The evil eye; also one's gaze or way of seeing. The belief that envy can cause harm through looking.
Fun; the Thai belief that whatever you do should have an element of enjoyment. Life should be sanuk.
Hand-feeding someone; the Ethiopian custom of putting food directly into another's mouth as a sign of love and respect.
Selfless hospitality; anticipating guests' needs without expecting anything in return. Service as an art form.
Hometown; ancestral home. More than geography—the place of origin that shapes identity, often idealized in memory.
The floating world; originally Buddhist term for earthly sorrows, later the pleasure quarters and ephemeral urban delights of Edo Japan.
The act of acquiring books and letting them pile up unread. A bibliophile's guilty pleasure.
terms.etymology: From 積む (tsumu, to pile up) + 読 (doku, reading)

terms.definition: The traditional custom of enjoying the transient beauty of flowers, especially cherry blossoms. A celebration of impermanence.
terms.etymology: From 花 (hana, flower) + 見 (mi, viewing)

terms.definition: Relationships, connections — the network of mutual obligations that structures Chinese social and business life. Not corruption but social fabric. You cultivate guanxi; you owe and are owed. Transactions happen within relationships, not between strangers.

True feeling and façade — the distinction between one's real opinion (honne) and public presentation (tatemae). Not hypocrisy but social lubrication. Everyone knows everyone's performing; that's the point. Harmony over authenticity.
Death from overwork — dying from work-related stress, heart attack, or suicide. A recognized cause of death in Japan since 1987. The dark side of dedication. The salary man's occupational hazard.
Outside person — foreigner, non-Japanese. Slightly rude; gaikokujin is more polite. The permanent category for those who can never fully belong, no matter how long they stay or well they speak.

Theories of Japaneseness — the genre of literature explaining Japanese uniqueness. Usually self-congratulatory, sometimes insightful, always essentialist. The cultural nationalism that says Japan is different because Japan is Japan.

Senior-junior — the hierarchical relationship structuring Japanese schools, companies, and society. Senpai guides and protects; kōhai respects and follows. Age or entry date determines rank. Vertical society made explicit.
Human feeling — natural emotion, compassion, what the heart wants. Often conflicts with giri (duty). The star-crossed lovers torn between obligation and love: Japan's favorite tragedy.

Harmony — the supreme value in Japanese society. Avoid conflict, maintain group cohesion, suppress individual assertion. Article 1 of the 7th-century Constitution: 'Harmony is to be valued.' The collective over the self.
A building's caretaker/janitor. In Soviet times, also an informer—eyes of the state.
A sled drawn by three horses abreast. Also a trio, or a Soviet judicial panel.
A heated metal container for boiling tea water. The heart of Russian hospitality.
Soviet youth who embraced Western fashion and jazz in the 1950s. Rebels in pompadours.
Polish concept of honor: pride, dignity, keeping one's word. Central to szlachta identity.
Polish noble ideology claiming descent from Sarmatians. Distinctive dress, customs, pride.
The long outer robe of Polish nobility. National dress of the szlachta.
Czech pub: center of social life, democracy of the beer hall.
Beer. Czechs drink more per capita than any nation. Central to identity.
The good soldier who defeats the system by apparent idiocy. Czech survival strategy.
A Balkan tavern for coffee, rakija, music, and passionate conversation.
Bulgarian fire dancers who walk on embers in trance. Thracian survival.
Ukrainian embroidered shirt. Regional patterns identify origins.
Slavic house spirit. Protects the home if respected.
Slavic witch who lives in a hut on chicken legs. Ambiguous: danger or help.
Slavic water spirit, often a drowned maiden. Dangerous beauty.
Slavic midsummer festival: bonfires, water, fern-flower seeking.
A bending of the knees with the back held straight. The foundation of ballet technique, used to warm up and as preparation for jumps.
Rising to the balls of the feet or full pointe. From French 'raised'—the dancer lifts against gravity.
A dance for two, typically a ballerina and male partner, showcasing both virtuosity and partnership. The romantic centerpiece of classical ballet.
A pose on one leg with the other extended behind. Named for its resemblance to Arabic decorative patterns—a body made ornamental.
A turn in which the working leg whips around to provide momentum. The 32 fouettés in Swan Lake are a legendary test of technique.
Dancing on the tips of the toes in reinforced shoes. The ethereal, gravity-defying image of ballet—achieved through years of training and pain.
The horizontal rail used for support during ballet warm-up exercises. Every ballet class begins at the barre before moving to center work.
Japanese avant-garde dance: white-painted bodies, grotesque slowness. Post-Hiroshima body.
Classical Tamil dance: precise geometry, storytelling, temple origins.
North Indian classical dance: footwork, spins, Mughal court elegance.
Odia classical dance: tribhanga pose, temple sculpture come alive.
Telugu classical dance-drama. Brass plate dancing.
Northeastern Indian dance: fluid, circular, devotional.
Kerala classical dance: graceful, feminine, swaying.
Hand gesture in Indian dance. Each tells a story. Hundreds of meanings.
Expression in Indian dance: face, body, emotion. Acting through movement.
Pure dance: rhythm and form without narrative meaning.
Expressive dance: movement conveying meaning and emotion.
Afro-Brazilian martial art disguised as dance. Acrobatics, music, roda circle.
The basic swaying step of capoeira. The root of all movement.
The circle of players in capoeira. Energy contained and exchanged.
Cuban-rooted Latin dance and music. Clave rhythm, partner work.
Dominican romantic music and dance. Hip motion, close embrace.
Dominican fast-tempo dance. Marching step, hip sway.
Colombian folk music and dance. African, indigenous, Spanish roots.
Argentine music and dance, ancestor of tango. Also a tango social dance.
Peruvian waltz: syncopated, romantic, distinct from European waltz.
1930s Harlem swing dance. Athletic, improvisational. Whitey's Lindy Hoppers.
Hip-hop athletic dance: toprock, downrock, freezes, power moves.
LA street dance: explosive, aggressive, expressive. Anger and joy.
Harlem ballroom dance: poses from fashion magazines. LGBTQ+ culture.
Disco-era arm-focused dance from LA gay clubs. Dramatic, musical.
Postmodern partner dance: sharing weight, following momentum. No steps.
English folk dance: bells, sticks, handkerchiefs. Ancient origins disputed.
Fast Southern Italian folk dance. Named for tarantula—dance out the bite.
Levantine line dance. Stomping, linked arms, celebration.
Mevlevi dervish spinning meditation. Arms outstretched, skirts flying.

Abu Dhabi's financial free zone — established 2015, operates under common law. Regulator is FSRA (Financial Services Regulatory Authority). Competes with DIFC for regional financial services. Located on Al Maryah Island.
terms.etymology: Abu Dhabi Global Market.

terms.definition: German stock corporation — the form for publicly traded companies. Requires minimum €50,000 share capital. Governed by AktG (Aktiengesetz). Has a two-tier board structure: Vorstand (management board) and Aufsichtsrat (supervisory board). Used throughout German-speaking countries.
terms.etymology: Aktien (shares, stocks) + Gesellschaft (company, society).

terms.definition: Unique identifier for EU legal documents — regulations, directives, decisions, case law. Format: sector + year + document type + number. Example: 32016R0679 is the GDPR. Used in EUR-Lex database. Essential for precise citation of EU law.
terms.etymology: Communitatis Europeae Lex — Latin for 'Law of the European Community'.

terms.definition: The statute governing corporations incorporated in Delaware — the most influential corporate law in America. More than 60% of Fortune 500 companies are Delaware corporations. Known for flexibility, predictable case law from the Court of Chancery, and business-friendly provisions.
terms.etymology: Delaware + General Corporation Law.

terms.definition: Dubai's financial free zone — operates under common law (based on English law), separate from UAE civil law. Has its own courts (DIFC Courts) and regulator (DFSA). Popular for regional headquarters, funds, and financial services. Companies can be 100% foreign-owned.
terms.etymology: Dubai International Financial Centre.

terms.definition: Standardized citation system for European court decisions. Format: ECLI:country:court:year:number. Example: ECLI:EU:C:2014:2454 (Google Spain). Enables uniform citation across jurisdictions. Adopted by CJEU, ECHR, and many national courts.
terms.etymology: European Case Law Identifier.

terms.definition: Let justice be done though the heavens fall. The principle that makes law something other than politics: the claim that justice must be done regardless of consequences, that the calculation of outcomes cannot override the obligation to act rightly. Both the formula and its critique have been active ever since: Kant endorsed it; Mill opposed it. The phrase identifies the fault line between deontological and consequentialist ethics, and between the rule of law and reason of state.
terms.etymology: Fiat (let it be done) + iustitia (justice) + ruat (let it fall) + caelum (heaven). Attributed to Ferdinand I, Holy Roman Emperor; popularised by Kant.

terms.definition: German limited liability company — the dominant form of German private company. Requires minimum €25,000 share capital. The most common corporate form in Germany, Austria, and Switzerland. Governed by the GmbHG (GmbH-Gesetz). Partners' liability limited to their capital contributions.
terms.etymology: Gesellschaft (company) + mit beschränkter (with limited) + Haftung (liability).

terms.definition: Independent legal reasoning. The process by which a qualified jurist derives a ruling from first principles (Quran, Hadith, analogy, consensus) rather than following established precedent. The door of ijtihad was said to have 'closed' around the 10th century — a claim disputed ever since. Islamic modernism is largely the argument that the door must be reopened.
terms.etymology: From jahada (to strive). Jihad shares the root — both are forms of strenuous effort.

terms.definition: American corporation designation — indicates a company incorporated under state law. C-Corps are taxed separately from shareholders; S-Corps pass through income. Delaware is the dominant state of incorporation for public companies due to its developed corporate law (DGCL).
terms.etymology: Incorporated — formally constituted as a legal corporation.

terms.definition: ICC rules defining buyer/seller responsibilities in international trade. Current version: Incoterms 2020. Key terms: EXW (Ex Works), FOB (Free on Board), CIF (Cost Insurance Freight), DDP (Delivered Duty Paid). Determines risk transfer point, who arranges transport/insurance, customs clearance responsibilities.
terms.etymology: International Commercial Terms — published by ICC since 1936.

terms.definition: American business structure combining corporate limited liability with partnership tax treatment. Flexible structure governed by state law. Members (not shareholders) own the company. Operating agreement defines governance. Delaware and Wyoming are popular formation states.
terms.etymology: Limited Liability + Company.

terms.definition: UK/US hybrid business form combining partnership flexibility with limited liability. Popular for professional services firms (law, accounting). Partners not personally liable for other partners' negligence. UK form governed by Limited Liability Partnerships Act 2000.
terms.etymology: Limited Liability + Partnership.

terms.definition: UK private limited company — cannot offer shares to the public. No minimum capital. The standard form for UK businesses. Governed by Companies Act 2006. Requires at least one director and one shareholder.
terms.etymology: Limited — referring to limited liability of shareholders.

terms.definition: UK public company — shares may be offered to the public and traded on stock exchanges. Minimum £50,000 share capital. Governed by Companies Act 2006. Must have at least two directors. Suffix 'plc' required in company name.
terms.etymology: Public (shares available to public) + Limited (liability) + Company.

terms.definition: Singapore private limited company — the dominant corporate form. Maximum 50 shareholders, shares not publicly traded. Minimum one director (Singapore resident), one shareholder, and company secretary. Governed by Companies Act. Registered with ACRA, assigned UEN (Unique Entity Number).
terms.etymology: Private Limited — Singapore adaptation of UK corporate terminology.

terms.definition: French public limited company — the form for large corporations and listed companies. Minimum €37,000 capital (€225,000 if publicly traded). Requires at least 7 shareholders. Two governance options: conseil d'administration or directoire with conseil de surveillance.
terms.etymology: Société anonyme — anonymous company, meaning shareholders are not personally liable.

terms.definition: French limited liability company — equivalent to GmbH or LLC. Partners' liability limited to contributions. Flexible structure for small and medium enterprises. Requires at least one associate (associé), no minimum capital since 2003.
terms.etymology: Société (company) + à responsabilité limitée (with limited liability).

terms.definition: French simplified joint-stock company — highly flexible corporate form popular for startups and subsidiaries. No minimum capital, great contractual freedom in organizing governance. The dominant form for venture-backed French companies.
terms.etymology: Société par actions (joint-stock company) + simplifiée (simplified).

terms.native: Uniform Customs and Practice for Documentary Credits
terms.definition: ICC rules governing letters of credit — the standard framework for documentary credits in international trade. Current version UCP 600 (2007). Defines obligations of issuing banks, confirming banks, beneficiaries. Universally adopted by banks worldwide.
terms.etymology: Uniform Customs and Practice + revision number 600.

terms.definition: Corporate structure used by Chinese companies to circumvent foreign investment restrictions. Offshore holding company (Cayman) controls onshore Chinese operating company through contracts rather than equity ownership. Used by most Chinese tech companies listed abroad (Alibaba, Baidu). Legal status uncertain under Chinese law.
terms.etymology: Variable Interest Entity — accounting term for controlled entities without majority voting interest.

terms.definition: Chinese company 100% owned by foreign investors — permitted in most industries since WTO accession. The standard structure for foreign subsidiaries in China. Registered as a limited liability company (有限责任公司) under Chinese law.
terms.etymology: Wholly Foreign-Owned + Enterprise.

terms.definition: Japanese limited liability company — equivalent to American LLC. Introduced in 2006 Companies Act. Flexible structure, no minimum capital. Popular for foreign subsidiaries and startups. Members (社員) manage the company.
terms.etymology: 合同 (gōdō: joint, combined) + 会社 (kaisha: company).

terms.definition: Japanese joint-stock company — the standard form for large Japanese corporations. Abbreviated KK. Minimum capital requirement abolished in 2006. Governed by the Companies Act (会社法). Listed companies trade on TSE (Tokyo Stock Exchange) within JPX.
terms.etymology: 株式 (kabushiki: shares) + 会社 (kaisha: company).

terms.definition: From the beginning — starting from first principles rather than inherited assumptions. In law: void from the start. In science: calculations from fundamental physics, not fitted data. The hard way, but the honest way.
In good faith — genuine, authentic, without intent to deceive. Legal term for honest dealing. Now colloquial: the real thing, not fake. A bona fide expert versus a pretender.
terms.etymology: Latin: bona (good) + fide (faith)

terms.definition: Let the buyer beware — the principle that purchasers bear risk for their decisions. Pre-consumer-protection doctrine. Still applies to used cars and NFTs. The seller's disclosure duty is modern pushback.
Body of the crime — the evidence that a crime occurred. Not the corpse (though that helps) but the fact of the offense. You cannot convict without proving something happened.
In fact — existing in practice, regardless of official status. De facto leader versus de jure leader. English is the de facto global language; no law made it so. Reality versus formality.
By law — officially sanctioned, legally recognized. The opposite of de facto. A constitution grants de jure rights; whether they exist de facto is another matter.
Let it be done — authoritative decree. Fiat lux: let there be light. Fiat money: currency by government declaration, not gold backing. Creation by command.

You shall have the body — the right to challenge unlawful detention. Produce the prisoner in court. The great writ against arbitrary imprisonment, dating to Magna Carta. Suspended in emergencies, to civil libertarians' horror.
By the fact itself — automatically, as a direct consequence. If you resign, you are ipso facto no longer employed. Causation built into the action.
With the necessary changes — once appropriate modifications are made, the argument applies. What holds for A holds for B, mutatis mutandis. The changes are assumed obvious.
By itself — intrinsically, without reference to other factors. 'Not illegal per se.' The thing considered alone, in its own nature.
At first face — on first appearance, before deeper investigation. Prima facie evidence: enough to proceed unless rebutted. The surface that may or may not hold up.
For good — professional services donated free, especially legal. Pro bono publico: for the public good. The profession's charitable obligation.
Something for something — mutual exchange, reciprocal benefit. In law: the consideration in a contract. In corruption: the bribe's explicit terms. Something given, something gotten.
Under judgment — currently before a court. Matters sub judice shouldn't be publicly discussed to avoid prejudicing proceedings. The case is open; wait for the verdict.
Unwelcome person — diplomatic term for expelled officials. More broadly: anyone banished from a group. You may exist, but not here.
Who benefits? — the investigator's first question. Follow the incentives. Cicero's legal principle: who profits from the crime? The conspiracy theorist's mantra.
The law is harsh but it is the law — legal positivism's slogan. We may dislike it; we must obey it. The tension between legality and justice.
Ignorance of the law is no excuse — you're bound by laws you don't know exist. Otherwise everyone claims ignorance. Brutal when laws are complex and countless.
In blazing offense — caught in the act, red-handed. Originally: while the crime is burning. Now often euphemism for sexual discovery. The undeniable evidence of presence.
Law of retaliation — eye for an eye. Hammurabi's code, Biblical justice. Actually a limit on revenge: only an eye, not a life. Proportionality as progress.
Guilty mind — the mental element of crime: intent, knowledge, recklessness. Without mens rea, usually no crime. You didn't just do it; you meant to.
Guilty act — the physical element of crime, contrasted with mens rea. You must both do the deed and intend it. Thoughts alone aren't crimes.
The thing speaks for itself — when the accident couldn't happen without negligence. A surgeon leaves a sponge inside. No expert needed; the facts scream.
To stand by decided matters — the doctrine of precedent. Courts follow prior rulings. Stability over correctness. Until it's overturned.

Korean family-controlled conglomerate — Samsung, Hyundai, LG, SK. Characterized by cross-shareholdings, diversification across unrelated industries, and close ties to government. The chaebol system drove Korea's rapid industrialization but also concentrates economic power in few families.
terms.etymology: 재 (jae: wealth) + 벌 (beol: clan, faction). Cognate with Japanese zaibatsu.

terms.definition: From before — based on prediction rather than outcome. Ex ante analysis: before the fact. Economists' favored perspective: judge decisions by information available at the time, not hindsight.
From after — based on actual outcomes. Ex post analysis: after the fact. Hindsight is 20/20, which is why ex ante evaluation matters.
By head — per person. GDP per capita: wealth divided by population. The measure that adjusts for scale, revealing intensity rather than totality.

Financial clique — the industrial conglomerates that built modern Japan: Mitsubishi, Mitsui, Sumitomo, Yasuda. Family-controlled pyramids of companies. Officially dissolved after WWII, effectively reconstituted as keiretsu.

System, series — postwar business networks linking companies through cross-shareholding and long-term relationships. Horizontal (around a bank) or vertical (around a manufacturer). The successor to zaibatsu, without family control.

Going around the roots — informal consensus-building before formal decision. Prepare the ground, consult stakeholders, address objections privately. The meeting just ratifies what's already decided. Process as politics.
terms.etymology: From gardening: preparing roots before transplanting

terms.definition: Request for decision — the Japanese system where proposals circulate for approval stamps (hanko) from all affected parties. Slow, consensus-building, risk-diffusing. Nobody decides; everybody decides.

Excess return above the benchmark — the value a fund manager adds beyond market performance. Positive alpha: you beat the market. Negative alpha: you'd have done better with index funds. The grail every active manager seeks and most fail to find.

Volatility relative to the market — a stock with beta 1.5 moves 50% more than the index. High beta: more risk, more potential return. Low beta: defensive. The measure of systematic risk you can't diversify away.

Risk-free profit from price differences — buying low in one market, selling high in another simultaneously. In theory, arbitrageurs eliminate inefficiencies instantly. In practice, execution risk, transaction costs, and black swans eat arbitrageurs alive. LTCM learned this.

An unpredictable, high-impact event that experts rationalize in hindsight. Nassim Taleb's term: before Australia, all swans were white by definition. 9/11, 2008 crash, COVID: obvious in retrospect, invisible in prospect. Our models exclude what matters most.
A brief recovery in a declining market — even a dead cat bounces if dropped from high enough. The sucker's rally that tricks optimists before the next leg down. The relief that isn't.

Hold On for Dear Life — originally a typo in a 2013 Bitcoin forum post, now crypto gospel. Don't panic sell; diamond hands through the crash. The strategy that works until it doesn't. Also retronymed: Hold On for Dear Life.
Fear, Uncertainty, Doubt — negative information spread to drive prices down. Originally IBM's competitive tactic. In crypto: any bearish news is dismissed as FUD. The tribal epistemology of markets.

The broker's demand for more collateral when leveraged positions move against you. Deposit more or get liquidated. The moment leverage reverses from amplifier to executioner. The phone call that ends careers.
When short sellers are forced to buy to cover positions, driving prices higher, forcing more covering. A feedback loop of pain. GameStop 2021: retail traders versus hedge funds, memes versus models.
Borrowing in low-interest currency, investing in high-interest currency — pocketing the spread. Works until the borrowed currency spikes. Picking up nickels in front of steamrollers. The widow-maker.

The graph of interest rates across maturities — normally slopes up (long-term rates higher than short). Inverted yield curve: short rates exceed long. The recession predictor with an imperfect but impressive track record.
When futures prices exceed spot prices — the normal state for commodities with storage costs. Rolling futures contracts in contango bleeds money. The silent killer of commodity ETFs.
When spot prices exceed futures prices — supply shortage, immediate demand. The opposite of contango. Rolling futures in backwardation generates positive roll yield. The rare favorable condition.

The ease of buying or selling without moving the price — cash is perfectly liquid; real estate isn't. Liquidity vanishes precisely when you need it. Everyone heads for the exit at once, and the door shrinks.

Using borrowed money to amplify returns — and losses. 10x leverage: 10% gain becomes 100%, 10% loss wipes you out. The tool that makes fortunes and destroys them. Every crisis has leverage at its heart.

Financial instruments whose value derives from underlying assets — options, futures, swaps. Used to hedge risk or to speculate with leverage. Warren Buffett: 'financial weapons of mass destruction.' Also: essential market infrastructure.
Valuing assets at current market prices rather than purchase price — honest but volatile. When markets freeze, there is no market to mark to. The accounting that turns paper losses into real ones.

When insurance against risk encourages risk-taking — banks that expect bailouts gamble bigger. The more protected you are from consequences, the more recklessly you act. Every safety net creates perverse incentives.

When one party has information the other lacks, and this distorts who participates — sick people buy health insurance, lemons get sold. Markets unravel when information asymmetry is severe. Akerlof's insight.

A state where no one can be made better off without making someone worse off — the economist's criterion of optimality. Says nothing about fairness: slavery could be Pareto efficient. Necessary but not sufficient.

Value destroyed by market distortions — the transactions that don't happen because of taxes, monopolies, or price controls. The area of the triangle economists love to draw. Inefficiency made geometric.

Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation, and Amortization — the profitability metric that ignores financing and accounting choices. Loved by private equity, mocked by Buffett: 'Does management think the tooth fairy pays for capital expenditures?'

The premium paid above book value in acquisitions — the accounting entry for overpaying. Supposedly represents brand value, synergies, intangibles. Often written down years later when the deal sours. The graveyard of M&A optimism.
Central bank buying assets to inject money into the economy — printing money with extra steps. QE1, QE2, QE∞. The policy that worked until it caused inflation. The monetary experiment of the 2010s.
Market panic when central banks hint at reducing stimulus — the 2013 bond selloff when Bernanke mentioned tapering. Addicts don't like hearing about withdrawal. The market's dependency exposed.
Trading ahead of client orders using inside knowledge — illegal for brokers, gray area for high-frequency traders who detect order flow. The parasitic extraction that erodes trust.
Artificially inflating an asset's price through misleading hype, then selling. The classic stock fraud, now endemic in crypto. The telegram group that makes insiders rich and followers poor.
Buying overpriced assets expecting to sell to someone even less informed — the logic of bubbles. You're not the fool if you sell first. Musical chairs with money. Works until the music stops.
Nourishing mother — one's school or university. Originally a Roman epithet for goddesses. The institution that fed your mind. Alumni return to the breast that raised them.
terms.etymology: Latin: alma (nourishing) + mater (mother)

terms.definition: Congratulatory tablet — the list of well-wishers in a festschrift. Academic gift-giving's social register. Who signed matters as much as what they wrote.
In the same place — abbreviation of ibidem. Citation shorthand: same source as previous footnote. The scholarly equivalent of 'ditto.'
Compare — abbreviation of confer. Citation instruction to compare with another source. Not 'see' but 'see and consider in relation to.'
Throughout, everywhere — citation indicating something appears in many places in a source. 'See Smith, passim.' Too frequent to cite individually.
Homesickness mixed with longing for the past; the Gaelic sense of exile from both place and time.
Vicarious embarrassment; feeling shame on behalf of someone else who should be—but isn't—embarrassed.
terms.etymology: From fremd (foreign, other) + schämen (to be ashamed)

terms.definition: The heart as seat of emotion and desire; deeper than kalp (physical heart). Where love, longing, and spiritual feeling reside.
Deep longing for someone or something absent; an ache of separation that is almost physical. The Turkish heart's way of keeping love alive across distance.
A deep longing for home, especially a home you cannot return to or that never was. The Welsh ache for the lost homeland of the soul.
The feeling of something missing; an awareness of absence or incompleteness that cannot be filled or named.
terms.etymology: From hiány (lack) + érzet (feeling)

terms.definition: Grief bacon; the weight gained from emotional overeating, especially during times of sorrow or stress.
terms.etymology: From Kummer (grief) + Speck (bacon/fat)

terms.definition: A state of torment created by the sudden sight of one's own misery. Kundera's untranslatable Czech concept.
Passionate interest or curiosity; also worry or concern for someone. The Turkish word captures both the light of fascination and the weight of caring.
The sensation of melting or being consumed by emotion, especially longing. An almost physical dissolution of self.
Romantic, passionate love—distinct from szeretet (affectionate love). An all-consuming passion that transforms and sometimes destroys.
To love with tenderness and pity; affection mixed with compassion. Deeper than yêu (romantic love).
Deep feelings; affection and emotional bonds between people. The Vietnamese emphasis on heartfelt connection.
A deep longing or yearning, especially for one's homeland, loved ones, or a lost past. The Polish ache for what is absent.
Grief, regret, and resentment combined; a specifically Polish sense of historical grievance and personal sorrow intertwined.
The spirit of joy, passion, and enthusiasm; a state of frenzy or high spirits, especially when celebrating or dancing.
A spiritual strain pushed to breaking point; the Dostoevskian state of intense feeling that tears the soul.
A deep, bittersweet melancholy that is almost pleasurable; the Slavic sense of longing and sadness that inspires poetry and song.
Sympathetic joy; taking delight in others' happiness and success. One of the four Brahmaviharas in Buddhist philosophy—the opposite of envy.
terms.etymology: From Sanskrit मुद् (mud, to be glad, rejoice)

terms.definition: The pain of separation from the beloved; longing that intensifies love through absence. Central theme in Indian poetry.
Bittersweet memory; a musical mode and feeling of nostalgic longing central to Ethiopian culture.
Nostalgic in a warm, fond way; the bittersweetness of happy memories. Not sad longing but affectionate remembrance.
A collective feeling of unresolved resentment, grief, and sorrow arising from injustice and oppression. Central to Korean cultural identity and artistic expression.
terms.etymology: From Classical Chinese 恨 (hàn, regret, resentment)

terms.definition: Serbian/Balkan feeling of blissful pleasure, especially from small things. Coffee, conversation.
Slovenian joy, delight—a bright, uncomplicated happiness.
Leather straps around a hawk's legs, attached to the leash.
A leather cap covering the hawk's eyes, keeping it calm.
The building housing hawks. Now often 'mews' for converted stables.
A wild-caught adult hawk. Harder to train. Now means gaunt.
A nestling hawk taken for training.
A male hawk, one-third smaller than the female.
Technically, a female falcon. Or broadly, the longwing family.
One who flies hawks (shortwings). Versus falconer (longwings).
A frame for carrying several hawks. Origin of 'cadger.'
A long training line attached to the hawk.
A falcon's hunting dive. Wings closed, maximum speed.
When a hawk attempts to fly from the fist, hanging by jesses.
To repair a broken feather by grafting in a piece.
When a hawk spreads wings over prey protectively.
A hawk in perfect hunting condition: keen, fit, ready.
When a hawk shakes and fluffs its feathers.
Setting a hawk outside on a perch. Exposure to elements.
The pellet of indigestible matter a hawk regurgitates.
A highly collected trot in place. Horse trots without advancing.
An elevated, cadenced trot with suspension. Floating movement.
'High school': advanced dressage movements. The art above.
Horse raises forequarters, hindquarters deeply bent. Classical air.
Horse leaps forward on hind legs. An 'air above the ground.'
Horse leaps, kicks hind legs straight back at height of jump. Most difficult air.
A 360-degree turn on the haunches at canter or walk.
Lateral movement: horse moves forward and sideways, bent toward direction.
Changing canter lead in the air, without breaking gait.
Shifting weight to hindquarters, lightening forehand. Self-carriage.
Controlled forward energy. Not speed—contained power.
The connection between rider's hand and horse's mouth through reins.
Horse accepting contact, flexed at poll, working from behind.
Horse evading contact by raising head. A fault.
An exaggerated high-stepping walk, extending forelegs.
Classical movements where horse leaves the ground: capriole, courbette, levade.
The 22 trump cards: Fool to World. The soul's journey.
The 56 suit cards: Wands, Cups, Swords, Pentacles. Daily life.
'Secrets': the mysteries encoded in tarot.
Card 0: the beginning and end, innocence, leap of faith.
Card I: will, skill, manifestation. As above, so below.
Card II: intuition, mystery, the subconscious.
Card XVI: sudden upheaval, destruction, revelation.
The pattern in which cards are laid out. Celtic Cross, three-card.
A card chosen to represent the querent or question.
The person asking the question. The seeker.
A card appearing upside down, often modifying its meaning.
Page, Knight, Queen, King of each suit. Personalities or aspects.
The Book of Changes: 64 hexagrams, ancient Chinese oracle.
Six-line figure in I Ching, each line yin or yang.
Traditional method for casting I Ching. 50 stalks, complex sorting.
Norse alphabet used for divination. Each rune has meaning.
The runic alphabet, named for first six letters.
Divination by earth: random marks generating figures. Arabic origin.
Roman divination by bird behavior. Reading the sky.
Divination by examining animal entrails. Etruscan practice.
Seeing visions in reflective surfaces: crystal ball, water, mirror.
Reading tea leaves or coffee grounds.
Reading character and future from hand lines. Chiromancy.
Seeking guidance by opening a book to a random passage.
The ten emanations through which Ein Sof reveals itself. The Tree of Life.
'Without end': the infinite, unknowable divine. Before emanation.
Diagram of the ten sephirot and 22 paths. Map of creation.
'Crown': the first sephirah. Closest to Ein Sof, pure will.
'Kingdom': the tenth sephirah. Physical reality, manifestation.
'Repair': mending the world's brokenness through righteous action.
Divine contraction: God withdrew to make room for creation.
'Shells': husks concealing divine sparks. Obstacles to holiness.
Numerical value of Hebrew words revealing hidden connections.
Creating words from first or last letters of a phrase. Kabbalistic acronyms.
Letter substitution revealing hidden meanings. Cipher mysticism.
Four levels of Torah interpretation: Peshat, Remez, Derash, Sod.
'Splendor': foundational Kabbalistic text. Mystical commentary on Torah.
'Book of Formation': early Kabbalistic text on creation through Hebrew letters.
The divine chariot of Ezekiel's vision. Early Jewish mysticism.
'Cleaving': mystical communion with God. Hasidic goal.

The here and now of an artwork — its unique existence at the place where it happens to be, the history inscribed in its material presence. Benjamin's concept in The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction: technical reproduction destroys the aura by detaching the reproduced object from the domain of tradition. The painting in a museum has aura; its postcard does not. The concept is simultaneously a loss (of ritual, of uniqueness) and a liberation (the politicisation of art freed from its cultic function).
