terms.etymology: Greek and Latin: breath, breeze, the barely perceptible emanation from an object.

quotes.text: Was im Zeitalter der technischen Reproduzierbarkeit verkümmert, ist die Aura des Kunstwerks.
quotes.source: Walter Benjamin, Das Kunstwerk im Zeitalter seiner technischen Reproduzierbarkeit, 1935

terms.definition: The everyday — the material texture of ordinary life. The Russian avant-garde's great enemy and great project: the Constructivists, Productivists, and LEF group wanted to transform byt — to revolutionise not just politics but the chairs, the teapots, the daily rituals of existence. The revolution would be incomplete until the logic of the old world was removed from the domestic sphere. Byt absorbed the revolution; the revolution failed to transform byt. The concept later became central to the Situationist International's concept of "everyday life."
terms.etymology: Russian: way of life, daily routine, the everyday. From byt' (to be).

terms.definition: The dark spirit of art. Lorca's concept: the mysterious force that animates great flamenco, bull-fighting, and poetry — not inspiration, not charm, but a kind of wound, a nearness to death. The duende cannot be summoned by technique alone; it comes only when the artist is at the edge. 'All that has dark sounds has duende.' It is the aesthetic force that confronts the problem of death rather than decorating it.
terms.etymology: From Spanish folk tradition: a goblin or spirit who inhabits a house. Lorca theorised it in Juego y teoría del duende (1933).

terms.definition: The verbal description of a visual work — language competing with image. Homer's description of Achilles' shield is the paradigm: the poem makes you see what cannot be seen, generates a world from words alone. The technique is both ancient exercise and modernist obsession: Keats's Ode on a Grecian Urn, Auden's Musée des Beaux Arts. Ekphrasis raises the question that haunts all representation: can language capture what only image can show, can image capture what only language can say?
terms.etymology: Greek: ek (out) + phrazein (to speak, to express). A complete, vivid description.

quotes.text: On it he made the earth and sky and sea, the weariless sun, the moon at the full, and all the signs that crown the heavens.
quotes.source: Homer, Iliad, XVIII (on the Shield of Achilles)

terms.definition: The point in space that contains all other points. Borges's 1945 story: in the basement of a house on Garay Street, Buenos Aires, the narrator sees the Aleph — a small iridescent sphere of about two or three centimetres, in which the entire universe is visible simultaneously, from every angle, without confusion. Not a metaphor. The Aleph is the paradox of the infinite contained in the finite — the library that contains all books, the map at 1:1 scale. The name of this project.
terms.etymology: First letter of the Hebrew alphabet — א — also the first infinite cardinal number in Cantor's set theory (ℵ₀). The point where language, mathematics, and mysticism converge.

terms.definition: Vivid bringing-before-the-eyes — making the absent present through speech. The rhetorical ideal of vividness: the description so precise that the listener sees the scene as if present. Quintilian: evidentia, the quality of making absent things apparent. Distinct from simple clarity: enargeia is the force that makes language cross the threshold from statement to experience. Benjamin's dialectical image and Barthes's punctum are its modern descendants.
terms.etymology: Greek: en (in) + argos (shining, bright). The word that is also at the root of "energy."

terms.definition: Half-timbered house. The building type where the structural skeleton is exposed — timber frame visible, spaces filled with wattle or plaster. A technology of honesty: the structure is the ornament. Ruskin would have approved. The aesthetic that refuses to hide how a thing is made.
terms.etymology: Fachwerk (framework, from Fach — panel + Werk — work) + Haus (house).

terms.definition: Total work of art; a synthesis of all art forms (music, drama, poetry, visual arts) into a unified aesthetic experience.
terms.etymology: Gesamt (total) + Kunst (art) + Werk (work)
terms.usage: Wagner conceived his operas as Gesamtkunstwerke that would transform society.

terms.definition: Imitation, representation. The founding concept of Western aesthetics — art as the imitation of nature or action. Plato distrusted it: the painter imitates appearances which are themselves imitations of Forms. Aristotle rehabilitated it: through mimesis, tragedy achieves catharsis. The entire debate about whether art represents or creates reality turns on this word.
terms.etymology: From mimeisthai (to imitate). The mime, mimic, and mnemonic share the root.

terms.definition: The infinite mirror. Heraldic term for a shield bearing a smaller image of itself — extended by André Gide to literature: the work that contains a representation of itself within itself. Hamlet's play-within-a-play. Las Meninas. The footnote that comments on its own footnote. The device that makes the frame visible.
terms.etymology: From the heraldic expression for placing a figure 'in the abyss' of a shield — i.e., at its centre.

terms.definition: Coquettish withdrawal that demands pursuit. The beloved's power to withhold — knowing that withdrawal intensifies desire. In the ghazal tradition, nāz is not cruelty but a structural feature of love: the lover requires the obstacle. Extended politically: the sovereign's nāz is the refusal of easy access that produces reverence. The opposite is niyāz — the lover's need, the supplicant's submission. The two terms define the entire axis of Persian lyric.
terms.etymology: Persian. Cognate with Sanskrit nāṭya (performance). The concept has no Western equivalent.

terms.definition: Defamiliarisation — making the habitual strange. Shklovsky's concept in Art as Technique (1917): the purpose of art is to restore the sensation of life, to make us feel things rather than merely recognise them. Habit kills perception; art kills habit. Tolstoy describes a flogging as if seeing it for the first time, without the softening of familiarity. Brecht's Verfremdungseffekt is its theatrical version: the actor who reminds the audience they are watching a play, preventing the comfortable identification that produces passive consumption.
terms.etymology: From stranny (strange, odd) + the prefix o- (making something). Shklovsky coined it in the manifesto Iskusstvo kak priyom.

quotes.text: Цель искусства — дать ощущение вещи как видение, а не как узнавание.
quotes.source: Viktor Shklovsky, Art as Technique, 1917

terms.definition: The specifically Russian category of the vulgarly self-satisfied — kitsch that does not know it is kitsch, banality pleased with itself, the false and the sham presenting themselves as the real and the refined. Nabokov: "a special kind of smug, philistine vulgarity." Not mere bad taste but the complacent enjoyment of second-hand emotions and borrowed ideas, the aesthetic and ethical failure of a person who does not notice their own shallowness. Gogol is the great anatomist of poshlost'.
terms.etymology: Old Russian poshlyi: ordinary, common. The word degraded from "common" to "vulgar" to "smug-vulgar."

quotes.text: Poshlost is not only the obviously trashy but mainly the falsely important, the falsely beautiful, the falsely clever, the falsely attractive.
quotes.source: Vladimir Nabokov, Nikolai Gogol, 1944

terms.definition: The aesthetic theory of emotional essences. Bharata's Nāṭyaśāstra identifies eight permanent emotional states (sthāyibhāvas) — love, humour, compassion, fury, heroism, terror, disgust, wonder — that art distils into pure aesthetic experience. The ninth rasa (śānta, tranquillity) was added by Abhinavagupta. Rasa is neither the emotion itself nor its representation but the generalised, purified essence that the connoisseur (rasika) experiences — a disinterested aesthetic enjoyment impossible in ordinary life. Abhinavagupta connects it to liberation (moksha).
terms.etymology: Sanskrit: juice, essence, taste. The metaphor is gustatory: aesthetic experience as flavour.

terms.definition: The taste of a place. Originally wine: the specific combination of soil, climate, slope, and microclimate that makes a Burgundy untranslatable. Extended to cheese, bread, language, character — the claim that place is not background but ingredient. Against globalisation's axiom that the particular can always be reproduced elsewhere.
terms.etymology: From terre (earth, land). First used in viticulture; generalised in the 20th century.

terms.definition: To do something with soul, creativity, or love; to put a piece of yourself into your work. The essence of devotion to craft.
terms.etymology: From Turkish merak (passion, strong interest)

terms.definition: Musical ecstasy; a state of enchantment and emotional transformation induced by music. The moment when performer and audience become one in shared rapture.
terms.etymology: From Arabic طرب (ṭarab, joy, delight, music)

terms.definition: The woven basket aesthetic; things imperfect but functional and beautiful in their simplicity.
An aesthetic centered on the acceptance of transience and imperfection; finding beauty in simplicity, asymmetry, and the weathered or incomplete.
terms.etymology: Wabi (rustic simplicity) + sabi (the beauty of age and wear)
terms.usage: Wabi-sabi influences tea ceremony, pottery, and garden design.

terms.definition: The bittersweet awareness of impermanence; a gentle sadness at the passing of things. The root of mono no aware.
The art of repairing broken pottery with gold lacquer, treating breakage as part of the object's history rather than something to disguise. Philosophically: embracing flaws and imperfections.
terms.etymology: From 金 (kin, gold) + 継ぎ (tsugi, joining)

terms.definition: The philosophy behind kintsugi: that broken things can become more beautiful for having been broken.
Negative space; the pause between notes, the emptiness between objects. In Japanese aesthetics, ma is not absence but a meaningful interval that gives shape to the whole.
terms.etymology: From 間 (ma, space, interval, pause)

terms.definition: Respect; deep reverence especially for elders and tradition. Foundation of Xhosa social harmony.
Nobility obligates; the idea that privilege entails responsibility. Those born to wealth and power have a duty to act generously and honorably.
terms.etymology: From Old French, literally 'nobility obliges'
terms.usage: The concept of noblesse oblige underpinned aristocratic paternalism.

terms.definition: Character, essence, moral nature. 'Ìwà l'ẹwà' (character is beauty)—the Yoruba belief that good character matters most.
Love of strangers; sacred hospitality. The ancient Greek duty to welcome and protect guests, considered a divine law.
terms.etymology: From φίλος (filos, friend) + ξένος (xenos, stranger)

terms.definition: What a waste! The sense that wasting anything—food, time, potential—is a shame. A Japanese environmental ethic.
An aperitivo that becomes dinner; extended pre-dinner drinks with enough snacks to skip the meal.

Everything in its place — the chef's discipline of preparing and organizing all ingredients before cooking. Not just efficiency but mindset: the calm that comes from readiness. Chaos controlled through preparation.
Under vacuum — cooking food sealed in plastic at precise low temperatures for extended periods. Perfect doneness edge-to-edge. The technique that modernist cuisine mainstreamed. Patience as method.
terms.etymology: French: sous (under) + vide (vacuum)

terms.definition: Savory deliciousness — the fifth taste, beyond sweet, sour, salty, bitter. Glutamates in parmesan, soy sauce, tomatoes, mushrooms. Identified by Ikeda in 1908, dismissed by the West until recently. The taste that makes food satisfying.

The chemical browning that creates flavor — amino acids and sugars reacting under heat. Bread crust, seared steak, roasted coffee. Not caramelization (that's just sugar). The reaction that makes cooked food taste cooked.
To deglaze — adding liquid to a hot pan to dissolve the caramelized fond stuck to the bottom. Wine, stock, even water. The technique that turns brown bits into sauce. Waste not, want not.

Foundation — both the caramelized bits on the pan (fond de cuisson) and the stock base of sauces (fond de cuisine). French cooking builds layers: protein leaves fond, liquid captures it, sauce emerges. Architecture of flavor.

The five mother sauces of classical French cuisine — béchamel, velouté, espagnole, hollandaise, tomate. Escoffier's taxonomy: master these and derive hundreds of variations. The grammar of French cooking.
Matchstick cut — vegetables sliced into thin, uniform strips. Precision as technique. Along with brunoise, chiffonade, and others: the knife skills that separate amateur from professional.
Fine dice — vegetables cut into tiny 3mm cubes, often starting from julienne. The smallest standard cut. Uniformity ensures even cooking. The meditation of knife work.
Ribbon cut — leafy herbs or greens rolled and sliced into thin strips. Basil over pasta, lettuce as garnish. The elegant finish.
Water bath — cooking or warming via a container set in hot water. Gentle, indirect heat. For custards, chocolate, delicate sauces. Also: the steam table keeping brunch warm.
To blanch — briefly boiling then shocking in ice water. Sets color, removes bitterness, loosens skins, par-cooks. The technique that makes vegetables vibrant green.
Preserved by slow-cooking in fat — duck legs submerged in duck fat, garlic in oil. Pre-refrigeration preservation that happens to be delicious. The texture that falls off the bone.
terms.etymology: French: confire (to preserve)

terms.definition: To braise — searing then slow-cooking covered in liquid. Breaks down tough cuts into tender. The alchemy of time: collagen becomes gelatin, sinew becomes silk. Peasant cooking elevated to art.

A stable mixture of immiscible liquids — oil and water held together by lecithin or other emulsifiers. Mayonnaise, hollandaise, vinaigrette. The chemistry that makes sauces creamy. Break the emulsion: greasy disaster.
A vineyard or group of vineyards recognized for quality, especially in Burgundy and Bordeaux. Grand cru denotes the highest classification.
A legally defined geographic region for wine production, guaranteeing origin and often production methods. The terroir made official.
A trained wine professional, typically in a restaurant, who specializes in wine service and food pairing. From Old French for 'pack animal driver'.
Naturally occurring polyphenols in grape skins, seeds, and oak barrels that create astringency and structure in wine. The 'grip' you feel.
The complex aromas that develop in wine through aging, as opposed to primary fruit aromas. A mature wine's olfactory signature.
The streaks of wine that run down the inside of a glass after swirling. Indicates alcohol and glycerol content, not quality despite the myth.
The formal description of a coat of arms in heraldic language. A precise technical vocabulary that can recreate any design from text alone.
The heraldic term for silver or white. One of the two 'metals' in heraldry, along with or (gold).
The heraldic term for red. From Old French goules (red fur neckpieces). One of the five traditional 'colours'.
The left side of a shield (from the bearer's perspective, right from viewer's). Latin for 'left'—hence the word's ominous connotations.
An animal lying down with head raised, alert. Contrasts with dormant (sleeping) and passant (walking).
An animal rearing up on its hind legs in profile, forepaws raised. The most aggressive heraldic posture—lions rampant are ubiquitous.
The complete armorial display: shield, helmet, crest, mantling, supporters, motto. The full heraldic statement.
The shield on which arms are displayed. The heraldic canvas. Also a small shield within a larger one.
The background of a shield, before any charges are placed. The tincture of the field is named first in a blazon.
Any emblem or figure placed on the field of a shield. Lions, eagles, crosses, crescents—all are charges.
A basic geometric charge: fess (horizontal bar), pale (vertical bar), bend (diagonal), chief (top third).
A horizontal band across the middle of the shield, typically one-third its height. A fundamental ordinary.
A vertical band down the center of the shield. The fess turned sideways.
A diagonal band from upper dexter to lower sinister. A bend sinister goes the other way—not illegitimacy, despite the myth.
The upper third of the shield, treated as a charge. 'In chief' means in this top section.
An inverted V-shaped ordinary. Represents rafters of a house—hence association with builders and protection.
A diagonal cross, like an X. St. Andrew's cross. The Scottish flag is a white saltire on blue.
A vertical and horizontal band intersecting at the center. Hundreds of variant crosses exist in heraldry.
A border around the edge of the shield. Often used to mark cadency—a difference between family branches.
A small square in the upper dexter corner of the shield. Often bears a secondary emblem.
One fourth of a shield, when divided by a cross. Quartering combines arms from different lineages.
The colors used in heraldry. Metals (or, argent), colours (gules, azure, vert, sable, purpure), and furs.
Gold in heraldry, typically depicted as yellow. One of the two metals. From French/Latin for gold.
Blue in heraldry. From the Arabic for lapis lazuli. One of the five traditional colours.
Green in heraldry. From French for green. Relatively rare as a field color.
Black in heraldry. Named for the black fur of the sable animal.
Purple in heraldry. The rarest of the traditional colours, as purple dye was historically expensive.
A fur pattern: black spots on white, representing ermine winter pelts. Symbol of royalty and nobility.
A fur pattern of alternating blue and white shield-shapes, representing squirrel pelts. Cinderella's slippers may have been vair, not 'verre' (glass).
The right side of a shield from the bearer's viewpoint (left as you look at it). The more honorable side.
An animal walking, three paws on the ground, one forepaw raised. The typical posture of the English lions.
An animal standing with all four feet on the ground. Alert but not in motion.
An animal sitting on its haunches, forepaws on the ground. Lions sejant are less common than rampant.
An animal looking backward over its shoulder. Added to any posture—'passant regardant', 'rampant regardant'.
An animal looking outward at the viewer. The English royal lions are 'passant guardant'.
A bird shown with wings spread and tips upward. The imperial eagle is always displayed.
A fish swimming horizontally across the shield.
A fish swimming vertically, head upward, as if rising to breathe.
The system of marks distinguishing junior branches of a family. Labels, crescents, mullets—each child's difference.
A horizontal bar with hanging points, mark of the eldest son during his father's lifetime.
A star, typically five-pointed, representing a spur rowel. Mark of the third son.
A half-moon with horns pointing upward. Mark of the second son.
A bird without feet, representing a swift or martin. Mark of the fourth son.
A ring. Mark of the fifth son.
Cloth draped from the helmet, often shown slashed and flowing. Originally protected armor from sun and rain.
A figure mounted on top of the helmet. Not the coat of arms itself—a common error.
A twisted roll of fabric between crest and helmet, in the principal colors. Also called a wreath.
Figures standing on either side of the shield, appearing to hold it up. Usually reserved for high nobility.
The base on which supporters stand—often a mound, waves, or symbolic ground.
A short phrase on a scroll, usually beneath the shield. War cries, moral principles, family sentiments.
Combining two coats of arms side by side on one shield, typically for marriage. Each squeezed to fit.
The arrangement of multiple coats of arms on a single shield, showing lineage and alliances.
The old order; the political and social system of France before the Revolution of 1789, characterized by monarchy, aristocratic privilege, and feudal vestiges.
terms.etymology: Ancien (old, former) + régime (system, order)
terms.usage: Tocqueville analyzed how the ancien régime's centralization persisted through revolution.

terms.definition: Forced coordination or synchronization; the Nazi process of bringing all aspects of German society into ideological conformity with the regime.
terms.etymology: Gleich (same, equal) + Schaltung (switching, circuit)
terms.usage: The Gleichschaltung systematically eliminated independent institutions, unions, and political parties.

terms.definition: Being in a foreign land; the state of exile or living away from home. Both the place and the feeling of displacement.
terms.etymology: From Arabic ghurba

terms.definition: The Roman Peace; the period of relative peace and stability across the Roman Empire from Augustus to Marcus Aurelius (27 BC - 180 AD).
terms.etymology: Pax (peace) + Romana (Roman)
terms.usage: The Pax Romana enabled commerce, cultural exchange, and the spread of Christianity.

terms.definition: The process of coming to terms with the past, particularly Germany's Nazi history. Encompasses public discourse, education, memorialization, and legal reckoning.
terms.etymology: Vergangenheit (past) + Bewältigung (coping, mastering)
terms.usage: Germany's Vergangenheitsbewältigung is often cited as a model for how nations can confront historical atrocities.
sources: Theodor Adorno - Was bedeutet: Aufarbeitung der Vergangenheit

terms.definition: Union; specifically the movement for unification of Cyprus with Greece, which dominated Cypriot politics until 1974.
terms.etymology: From Greek 'henosis' (union, oneness)
terms.usage: Enosis became a rallying cry during the anti-colonial struggle against Britain.

terms.definition: Freedom or Death; the motto of the Greek War of Independence (1821), embodying the absolute commitment to liberation from Ottoman rule.
terms.etymology: Eleftheria (freedom) + i (or) + thanatos (death)
terms.usage: The nine stripes of the Greek flag are said to represent the nine syllables of this phrase.

terms.definition: The Great Idea; the irredentist vision of reclaiming Constantinople and uniting Greek-speaking populations under a single state, dominant from independence to the Asia Minor catastrophe.
terms.etymology: Megali (great) + idea (idea)
terms.usage: The Megali Idea drove Greek foreign policy until the 1922 defeat.

terms.definition: The state of being in a foreign land; the Greek experience of emigration and the longing it creates.

Before the war — in American usage, before the Civil War. The slaveholding South's genteel self-image. 'Antebellum architecture' is a euphemism for plantation houses. History's temporal landmarks are often violent.
I came, I saw, I conquered — Caesar's boast after rapid victory at Zela. Three words, three acts, triumph compressed. The template for all subsequent mic drops.
The die is cast — Caesar crossing the Rubicon, committing to civil war. The point of no return. Action that cannot be undone. Every startup's Series A.

Middle Kingdom — China's name for itself: the center of civilization, the axis around which the world turns. Not ethnocentric arrogance but cosmological fact, in the traditional view. All else is periphery.
terms.etymology: Chinese: 中 (zhōng, middle) + 國 (guó, kingdom)

terms.definition: Imperial examination — China's meritocratic system for selecting officials, lasting from 605 to 1905. Confucian classics tested; peasants could theoretically rise to power. Created the scholar-gentry class. The world's first standardized testing regime.

Knocking the head — the prostration of kneeling and touching forehead to ground. The ultimate gesture of submission to emperor or ancestors. British refusal to kowtow in 1793 signaled coming collision of world orders.
terms.etymology: Chinese: 叩 (kòu, knock) + 頭 (tóu, head)

terms.term: 華夷之辨 (Huá Yí Zhī Biàn)
terms.definition: Hua-Yi distinction — the differentiation between civilized Chinese (Hua) and barbarians (Yi). Cultural rather than racial: barbarians could become Chinese by adopting civilization. The framework that ordered the tributary system.

Century of humiliation — the period from the Opium Wars (1839) to Communist victory (1949) when China suffered foreign imperialism, unequal treaties, and national weakness. The wound that still shapes Chinese foreign policy. Never again.

Taiping Heavenly Kingdom — the pseudo-Christian rebel state (1851-1864) whose civil war killed 20-30 million. Hong Xiuquan claimed to be Jesus's brother. The deadliest conflict of the 19th century, largely forgotten in the West.

Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution — Mao's campaign (1966-1976) to purge capitalist and traditional elements. Red Guards destroyed temples, persecuted intellectuals, sent millions to countryside. Chaos rebranded as revolution. Still officially '70% good, 30% bad.'

Great Leap Forward — Mao's catastrophic industrialization campaign (1958-1962). Backyard furnaces, collectivized farming, falsified statistics. Result: 15-55 million dead in famine. The gap between utopian planning and reality.

Cultivated talent — the lowest degree in the imperial examination system, granting local prestige and tax exemptions but not office. The entry level to the scholar-gentry. Success here meant years of study; failure was common.

Tent government — the shogunate, military government ruling Japan while the Emperor remained nominal sovereign. Kamakura, Ashikaga, Tokugawa: three bakufu spanning 1185-1868. The fiction of imperial rule, the reality of warrior power.
terms.etymology: Japanese: 幕 (maku, curtain) + 府 (fu, government)

terms.definition: Commander of forces — the military dictator ruling Japan in the Emperor's name. Sei-i Taishōgun: 'Great General Who Subdues Barbarians.' The title that became a government. Real power behind the chrysanthemum curtain.

Great name — feudal lords who ruled domains under the shogun. Controlled land, commanded samurai, collected taxes. Tokugawa kept them weak through sankin-kōtai. The balance of power that maintained 250 years of peace.

One who serves — the warrior class of feudal Japan, bound by bushidō. Originally guards, they became rulers. Abolished as a class in 1876 but mythologized ever since. The sword is the soul of the samurai.
terms.etymology: Japanese: saburau (to serve)

terms.definition: Drifting person — a masterless samurai, without lord or stipend. Shameful status, romantic image. The 47 Rōnin's revenge became Japan's favorite story. Now also: students who failed university entrance exams, adrift between attempts.

Alternate attendance — Tokugawa policy requiring daimyō to spend alternate years in Edo, leaving family as hostages. Bankrupted lords through travel costs, built roads, spread culture. Control through exhaustion.

Chained country — Japan's isolation policy (1633-1853), limiting foreign contact to Chinese and Dutch at Nagasaki. Christianity banned, Japanese forbidden to leave. Two centuries of peace and stagnation, ended by Perry's black ships.

Meiji Restoration — the 1868 revolution ending shogunate rule and restoring imperial power. Not restoration but revolution: feudalism abolished, modernization forced. Japan went from medieval to industrial in forty years. Transform or be colonized.

Enrich country, strengthen military — Meiji Japan's national slogan. Industrialize to build armies to protect against Western imperialism. It worked, then worked too well: the army that beat Russia in 1905 overreached in 1941.
Divine wind — the typhoons that destroyed Mongol invasion fleets in 1274 and 1281, saving Japan. In WWII, suicide pilots invoking that salvation. Nature's intervention recoded as human sacrifice.
terms.etymology: Japanese: 神 (kami, god) + 風 (kaze, wind)

terms.definition: Cutting belly — ritual suicide by disembowelment, the samurai's honorable death. Also called hara-kiri. Avoid capture, atone for failure, protest with your life. The ultimate statement of sincerity.

Elder statesmen — the informal council of Meiji oligarchs who chose prime ministers and guided policy behind the scenes. Constitutional fiction, real power. The last died in 1940; no one replaced them; Japan had no brakes.
Polish nobility: a large, politically powerful class with traditions of liberty.
Throwing someone out a window. Praguen specialty—started wars, ended careers.

A system capable of simulating any Turing machine — able to compute anything computable, given enough time and memory. Your laptop, JavaScript, Conway's Game of Life, PowerPoint, even Magic: The Gathering. The threshold beyond which all computers are equivalent in power, differing only in speed.

The impossibility of writing a program that determines whether any arbitrary program will halt or run forever. Proved undecidable by Turing in 1936. The first and most fundamental limit of computation. You cannot, in general, predict what programs will do without running them.

The class of problems where solutions are easy to verify but (probably) hard to find. If you solve one efficiently, you solve them all. Traveling salesman, satisfiability, scheduling — thousands of practical problems reduce to each other. P=NP? remains open; most believe P≠NP.

The future cost of taking shortcuts now — the interest you pay on expedient code. Coined by Ward Cunningham. Like financial debt: sometimes worth taking, always must be serviced. Unmaintained code accrues debt. Refactoring pays it down. Bankruptcy is the rewrite.

The chain of prerequisites that leads you far from your original task. You wanted to deploy, but first you need to update the config, but first you need to fix the script, but first you need to install a library, but first... now you're shaving a yak. Named by Carlin Vieri at MIT.

Explaining code line by line to an inanimate object (traditionally a rubber duck) to find bugs. The act of articulation forces clarity. Works because talking is slower than thinking and exposes assumptions. Any patient listener works; the duck need not understand.

Copying code without understanding why it works — ritual imitation without comprehension. Named after Pacific island cargo cults that built mock airstrips hoping planes would return. Stack Overflow syndrome: copy, paste, pray. Works until it doesn't.

A function that calls itself — the computational technique where a procedure is defined in terms of itself. Factorial: n! = n × (n-1)!. Elegant but dangerous: without base case, infinite loop. Hofstadter's strange loops. To understand recursion, first understand recursion.

A program that outputs its own source code — self-replication in minimal form. Named for logician Willard Van Orman Quine. The computational equivalent of 'this sentence.' Possible in any Turing-complete language. A proof that programs can describe themselves.

Giving disproportionate attention to trivial matters — named by Poul-Henning Kamp after Parkinson's example: a committee approves a nuclear reactor quickly but debates the bike shed for hours. We argue about what we understand. Also known as the law of triviality.

A bug that disappears or changes when you try to observe it — named for Heisenberg's uncertainty principle. Adding print statements changes timing. Running in debugger changes memory layout. The act of measurement disturbs the system.

A bug that is consistent and reproducible — named as contrast to Heisenbug, after Bohr's deterministic atomic model. It manifests reliably under the same conditions. The good kind of bug: you can study it, trap it, fix it.

Code that overuses strings where specific types would be safer — a pun on 'strongly typed.' Passing 'true' instead of true, user IDs as strings instead of typed wrappers, JSON everywhere. Convenient until runtime explodes. The type system can't help you.
'Compulsion to move': any move worsens your position. Being forced to self-destruct.
'In-between move': an unexpected interposed move before the expected one.
Developing a bishop to the long diagonal (b2/g2 or b7/g7).
'In passing': pawn captures another pawn that just moved two squares.
Sacrificing material, usually a pawn, for positional advantage.
One piece attacking two or more enemy pieces simultaneously.
Attacking a piece that cannot move without exposing a more valuable piece behind it.
Like a pin reversed: attacking a valuable piece that must move, exposing a lesser piece.
Moving one piece reveals an attack by another.
Special move: king and rook move simultaneously for king safety.
Player has no legal moves but isn't in check. Draw.
King is in check with no escape. Game over.
A very bad move, often losing material or the game.
A spectacular, unexpected, often sacrificial winning move.
A unit of time: one move. Gaining or losing tempo.
Having the attacking momentum, forcing opponent to react.
Getting pieces off their starting squares to active positions.
The final phase with few pieces remaining.
The phase after opening development, before endgame.
The initial moves, often following known theory.
Numerical skill rating. Named for Arpad Elo. 2800+ is elite.
1.e4 c5. Black's most popular and combative response.
A hypermodern defense: fianchettoed kingside bishop, counterattack.
A stone or group with only one liberty remaining. 'Check' in Go.
A position that could repeat infinitely. Rules prevent immediate recapture.
Having the initiative: opponent must respond. The tempo holder.
Losing the initiative: you must respond to opponent's move.
Established sequences in the corners. 'Set stones'—local equality.
The opening: spreading stones across the board. Whole-board strategy.
A skillful tactical move. 'Hand muscle'—the clever play.
'Taste': latent possibilities in a position. Potential not yet realized.
Light, flexible handling of stones in a difficult position. Graceful escape.
The form of connected stones. Good shape is efficient; bad shape is heavy.
An empty point adjacent to a stone. Stones need liberties to survive.
An empty point surrounded by your stones. Two eyes = life.
The study of which groups can live or will die.
Two equivalent options: if opponent takes one, you take the other.
Ignoring opponent's last move to play elsewhere. Strategic abandonment.
A neutral point belonging to neither player. Also: no good, useless.
Points given to White to compensate for Black playing first.
Amateur ranks, counting down. 30-kyu beginner to 1-kyu strong amateur.
The Go board: 19×19 lines. Also 9×9 and 13×13 for learning.
A suit designated to beat other suits. The master cards.
Attempting to win with a lower card by playing through an opponent.
Winning all tricks in a bridge hand. Maximum triumph.
Winning 12 of 13 tricks in bridge.
Having no cards in a suit. Opportunity to trump.
Having only one card in a suit.
Having exactly two cards in a suit.
Forcing opponent to discard a winning card. Endgame technique.
To fail to follow suit when able. Usually a penalty.
An offer to take a certain number of tricks, often in auction.
In bridge, the player who plays both their hand and dummy's.
In bridge, the hand laid face-up, played by declarer.
An onlooker offering unsolicited advice. Yiddish origin.
A card that can represent any other card. The joker.

Beautiful but unfaithful. The French 17th–18th century tradition of translation that adapted source texts to French taste — elegant, fluent, idiomatic — at the cost of the original's foreignness. Opposed to the German Romantic tradition (Schleiermacher, Hölderlin) that sought to let the foreign remain foreign, to bring the reader to the text rather than the text to the reader. The tension between domestication (belles infidèles) and foreignisation defines all translation ethics.
terms.etymology: The phrase attributed to Gilles Ménage (17th c.) of Nicolas Perrot d'Ablancourt's translations of ancient authors.

terms.definition: Gap, hole, pit. In textual scholarship: a missing or illegible portion of a manuscript. Extended: any gap in knowledge, argument, or record. The lacuna is not simply absence but absence with a shape — you can see where something was. Scholarship is largely the study of lacunae.
terms.etymology: From lacus (lake, pit). The medical term for a small cavity derives from the same root.

terms.definition: 'If only' or 'I wish'; expresses longing, hope, or acceptance. The Italian shrug of optimistic resignation.
Pig misery! A versatile Italian expletive expressing frustration, disbelief, or reluctant admiration.

Thus, so. The parenthetical that says: I know this looks wrong, but I am quoting accurately — the error belongs to the original. [sic] is the scholar's most precise gesture of distancing. It does not correct; it marks the boundary between the editor's responsibility and the text's. Every [sic] contains a judgment.
terms.etymology: Latin adverb sic (so, thus). Often written in brackets: [sic].

terms.definition: The limit before which / after which. Scholarly tools for dating: the terminus post quem is the earliest possible date (the thing cannot be earlier than X); the terminus ante quem is the latest possible date (it cannot be later than Y). Between the two termini lies the possible. All historical knowledge is framed by termini.
terms.etymology: Terminus (boundary, end point) + ante (before) / post (after) + quem (accusative of qui, which).

terms.definition: Translator traitor. The Italian pun that names the fundamental problem of translation: to translate is necessarily to betray — every choice to preserve one element (rhythm, meaning, tone, syntax) sacrifices another. The pun only works in Italian; its untranslatability is its argument. But the concept is more complex than simple loss: Borges argued that translations can improve on originals, that the Quixote is better in translation than in Cervantes. Every translator negotiates their treachery differently.
terms.etymology: Italian: traduttore (translator) / traditore (traitor). The two words share the Latin root tradere (to hand over, to betray).

quotes.text: The original is unfaithful to the translation.
quotes.source: Jorge Luis Borges, on Henley's translation of Beckford

terms.definition: 'Oh heavens!' An all-purpose exclamation of surprise, dismay, or exasperation. The Vietnamese sigh.

Translation and transference — the same word. Schleiermacher introduced the term for translation; Freud used it for the patient's displacement of earlier emotional attachments onto the analyst. The coincidence is not accidental: both translation and transference involve the transfer of something — meaning, affect — across a gap, with inevitable distortion. What arrives is not what departed. Derrida's essay "Des Tours de Babel" makes the connection explicit: translation is always a form of transference, never a transparent passage.
terms.etymology: Über (over, across) + tragen (to carry). The double meaning is native to the German word.

terms.definition: Language feeling — the intuitive sense of what sounds right in a language. Native speakers know when grammar is wrong even if they can't explain why. The linguistic ear. What grammar rules try and fail to fully capture.
terms.etymology: German: Sprache (language) + Gefühl (feeling)

terms.definition: And the rest — abbreviated etc. The admission that a list could continue but won't. Often a sign of vagueness: what exactly are the et cetera?
Namely — abbreviation of videlicet. Used to introduce specific examples or clarifications. 'Three continents, viz. Europe, Asia, Africa.' More formal than 'i.e.' or 'e.g.'

The smallest unit of sound that distinguishes meaning — /p/ and /b/ are different phonemes because 'pat' and 'bat' mean different things. The atoms of speech. Each language selects from the universal inventory.
The smallest unit of meaning — 'un-break-able' has three morphemes. Words decompose into meaningful pieces. The elements that combine into vocabulary.
How context shapes meaning — 'Nice weather we're having' during a storm. What's said versus what's meant. The study of implicature, speech acts, conversational norms. Language in use.
Words whose meaning depends on context — 'here,' 'now,' 'I,' 'this.' You can't interpret them without knowing who, where, when. The pointers that ground language in situation.
The rules governing sentence structure — word order, phrase structure, grammatical relations. Chomsky's domain. The difference between 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog.'
The study of meaning — what words and sentences mean, apart from how they're used. Truth conditions, reference, sense. 'That's just semantics' dismisses what actually matters.

Alternating between languages or dialects in conversation — switching to Spanish at home, professional English at work. Identity performed through linguistic choice. Everyone does it; bilinguals just do it more visibly.

A simplified language arising between groups with no common tongue — limited vocabulary, simplified grammar, used for trade. No native speakers. The makeshift bridge. If children grow up speaking it, it becomes a creole.
A pidgin that has become a native language — full complexity emerges in one generation. Haitian Creole, Tok Pisin. The proof that children don't just learn language; they create it.

A common language between speakers of different native tongues — originally the Mediterranean trade pidgin. Now English globally, Swahili in East Africa, Indonesian in its archipelago. The bridge language.
A word that appears only once in a corpus — occurring once in Shakespeare, once in the Bible. The translator's nightmare: context can't help. The lonely word.
A loan translation — borrowing a foreign expression by translating its parts. 'Skyscraper' becomes gratte-ciel (French), rascacielos (Spanish). The idea crosses; the sounds don't.
Words in different languages descended from the same ancestor — 'mother,' 'mater,' 'Mutter,' 'mère.' Shared heritage across millennia. The family resemblance that traces migrations.
Words that look similar across languages but differ in meaning — 'embarazada' (Spanish: pregnant) is not 'embarrassed.' The cognate that betrays. The translator's trap.

The fatal flaw — or more accurately, the tragic error. Aristotle's term for the hero's mistake that triggers catastrophe. Not a moral failing but a misjudgment. Oedipus' hamartia isn't pride but investigation. The translation as 'flaw' misleads.
terms.etymology: Greek: hamartanein (to miss the mark, to err)

terms.definition: Recognition — the moment in tragedy when the hero discovers the truth. Oedipus learning who he is. The reversal from ignorance to knowledge that triggers catastrophe or salvation. Aristotle considered it tragedy's most powerful device.
terms.etymology: Greek: anagnorizein (to recognize)

terms.definition: Reversal of fortune — the turning point where everything changes. Best when combined with anagnorisis: the recognition causes the reversal. The moment the messenger arrives. Plot structure's pivot.
terms.etymology: Greek: peri (around) + piptein (to fall)

terms.definition: Into the middle of things — beginning a narrative at a crucial point rather than at the beginning. Homer's technique: the Iliad opens in the war's tenth year. Flashbacks fill in context. The reader is dropped into action, hooked before understanding.
terms.etymology: Latin: in (into) + medias (middle) + res (things)

terms.definition: God from the machine — an unexpected power or event that solves an unsolvable problem. Named for Greek theater's crane that lowered gods onto stage. Now pejorative: a sign the writer couldn't resolve the plot. Convenient but unsatisfying.
terms.etymology: Latin: deus (god) + ex (from) + machina (machine)

terms.definition: It is sweet and fitting — from Horace: to die for one's country. Wilfred Owen called it 'the old Lie' after witnessing World War I gas attacks. The phrase that broke.
And you, Brutus? — Caesar's last words to his betraying friend (in Shakespeare). The ultimate expression of betrayal's wound: not just stabbed, but by you.

To the person — attacking the arguer instead of the argument. A fallacy when used to dismiss claims, but sometimes legitimate: credibility matters, and hypocrites can be called out. The fallacy is thinking 'bad person' implies 'wrong argument.'
terms.etymology: Latin: ad (to) + hominem (person)

terms.definition: Reduction to absurdity — disproving a proposition by showing it leads to ridiculous or contradictory conclusions. Euclid's method for proving infinity of primes. Socratic irony's structure. If your premises lead to nonsense, your premises are wrong.
terms.etymology: Latin: reductio (reduction) + ad (to) + absurdum (absurdity)

terms.definition: The way of affirming — the fundamental rule of inference: if P implies Q, and P is true, then Q is true. If it rains, the ground gets wet; it's raining; therefore the ground is wet. The workhorse of deductive logic.
terms.etymology: Latin: modus (way, method) + ponens (placing, affirming)

terms.definition: The way of denying — if P implies Q, and Q is false, then P is false. If it rained, the ground would be wet; the ground is dry; therefore it didn't rain. Falsification's logical structure. Popper's criterion of science.
terms.etymology: Latin: modus (way) + tollens (removing, denying)

terms.definition: Therefore — the logical connector. Cogito ergo sum. Often pretentious in English when 'so' would do. The word implies rigorous inference but is often used loosely.
It does not follow — a logical fallacy where the conclusion doesn't follow from premises. Also: an irrelevant statement. 'The weather's nice; therefore, raise my salary.' The gap between statements.
After this — the fallacy that sequence implies causation. Post hoc ergo propter hoc: after this, therefore because of this. The rooster crows, then the sun rises; the rooster doesn't cause dawn.
Without which not — an indispensable condition. Oxygen is sine qua non for fire. The necessary ingredient, the thing you cannot do without.
The position being reversed — with the order exchanged. A affects B and vice versa. Symmetry assumed, sometimes falsely.
Misrepresenting an argument to make it easier to attack — you argue against the caricature, not the position. The scarecrow you can knock down. Defeat an opponent who never showed up.
A distraction from the actual issue — the irrelevant point that derails debate. From training hunting dogs with smoked fish. Change the subject when you're losing.

You too — deflecting criticism by pointing to the accuser's hypocrisy. 'You criticize my emissions? You flew here.' The fallacy of avoiding substance through counter-accusation. Hypocrisy doesn't refute truth.

Claiming one step inevitably leads to extremes without justification — 'If we allow X, soon we'll have Y and Z.' Sometimes valid (precedent matters), often fallacious (steps are distinguishable). The paranoid argument.
Presenting only two options when more exist — 'You're with us or against us.' The excluded middle. Forcing a choice between extremes, ignoring nuance. Either/or thinking.

Assuming the conclusion in the premise — circular reasoning. 'God exists because the Bible says so, and the Bible is true because it's God's word.' The argument that proves nothing. Often misused to mean 'raises the question.'

Using an expert's opinion as proof — valid when the expert is relevant; fallacious when not. Einstein on physics versus Einstein on politics. Celebrity endorsements. The shortcut that sometimes works.
Assuming natural means good — arsenic is natural; vaccines aren't. The naturalistic fallacy. Evolution gave us cancer and cruelty. Nature is not a moral guide.
The strongest version of an opponent's argument — the opposite of straw man. Engage the best case, not the worst. Intellectual honesty as practice. If you can't steelman it, you don't understand it.
Defending a controversial claim by retreating to an uncontroversial one — the bailey is the bold position; the motte is the defensible retreat. 'I just meant...' after pushback. Strategic ambiguity.
Overwhelming opponents with quantity of arguments, regardless of quality — named for creationist Duane Gish. Each claim takes seconds to make, minutes to refute. The firehose of falsehood.
The right-hand side of a ship when facing forward. From Old English 'steorbord' (steering side), as the steering oar was traditionally mounted on the right.
terms.etymology: Old English steorbord

terms.definition: The left-hand side of a ship when facing forward. Originally 'larboard', changed to 'port' to avoid confusion with 'starboard' in verbal commands.
terms.etymology: From the loading port on the left side

terms.definition: A unit of length equal to six feet, used to measure water depth. Also means to understand deeply—to 'sound the depths' of a problem.
terms.etymology: Old English fæthm (outstretched arms)

terms.definition: The sideways drift of a ship downwind from its course. Metaphorically, the margin of freedom or flexibility in a situation.
terms.etymology: From lee (shelter from wind) + way

terms.definition: Shipboard gossip or rumors. Originally the cask of drinking water around which sailors would gather and chat—the ship's water cooler.
terms.etymology: From scuttle (hatch) + butt (cask)

terms.definition: A belt of calm winds near the equator where sailing ships could be stranded for weeks. Metaphorically, a state of stagnation or depression.
terms.etymology: Perhaps from Old English dol (dull)

terms.definition: A powerful whirlpool. From a specific tidal current off Norway's coast. Now denotes any turbulent, chaotic, or overwhelming situation.
terms.etymology: Dutch malen (to grind) + stroom (stream)

terms.definition: Toward the stern of a ship, behind. 'Abaft the beam' means behind an imaginary line across the ship's middle.
At right angles to the ship's length. A landmark 'abeam' is directly to the side, neither ahead nor behind.
A command to stop or cease. From Dutch 'houd vast' (hold fast). The sailor's imperative halt.
terms.etymology: Dutch houd vast

terms.definition: To secure a ship's hatches with strips of wood (battens) before a storm. Now means to prepare for any difficulty.
To secure a rope by winding it around a cleat or pin. Also a command to disregard a previous order.
The lowest internal part of a ship's hull where water collects. Bilge water is notoriously foul—hence 'bilge' as nonsense.
The stand housing the ship's compass, with correcting magnets and a light for night navigation. The navigator's altar.
A short thick post on a ship or wharf for securing mooring lines. The humble anchor point of enormous vessels.
Boatswain—the petty officer responsible for a ship's deck crew, rigging, and anchors. Pronounced 'BOH-sun'.
A spar extending forward from the bow, carrying forestays and sails. The ship's pointing finger.
A wall-like partition dividing a ship's interior into compartments. Critical for containing flooding and fire.
A vertical rotating machine for winding rope or chain, used for raising anchors. Sailors pushed its bars in endless circles.
Tilting a ship on its side to clean or repair the hull below the waterline. A vulnerable position—hence 'careening out of control'.
A beam projecting from the bow for raising and carrying the anchor. Named for the carved cat faces that often decorated them.
Sealing the seams between planks with oakum and pitch to make the hull watertight. An ancient shipwright's art.
A T-shaped fitting for securing ropes. Simple, elegant, essential—the grammar of the working deck.
A raised border around a hatch or cockpit to prevent water from entering. The ship's lips.
A stairway or ladder leading from the deck to the cabin below. The threshold between above and below.
Navigation by calculating position from speed, time, and course—without celestial observation. Deduced reckoning, corrupted to 'dead'.
The depth of water a ship needs to float. A ship 'draws' this much water. Deep draft limits where you can go.
A fitting that guides a rope, changing its direction without chafing. Invisible when working, obvious when absent.
A carved figure at the ship's prow. Once believed to appease sea gods; now means a leader without real power.
Wreckage floating after a shipwreck. Legally distinct from jetsam (thrown overboard intentionally). The sea's detritus.
Cargo deliberately thrown overboard to lighten a ship in distress. What we sacrifice to survive.
Forecastle—the forward part of a ship where crew quarters are located. Pronounced 'FOKE-sul'. Where sailors lived.
The distance from waterline to deck. More freeboard means a drier, safer ship; less means more cargo but more risk.
To roll and secure a sail to its yard or boom. The opposite of setting sail—putting the ship to sleep.
A ship's kitchen. Compact, efficient, rolling with the sea. The cook works in a space where nothing stays still.
A passage or ramp for boarding a ship. Also an order to clear the way—make a path!
The upper edge of a ship's side. Pronounced 'GUNN-ul'. Originally reinforced to support guns.
A rope for raising and lowering sails or flags. From 'haul yard'—pull the yard (the horizontal spar).
A thick rope or cable for mooring or towing. The heavy-duty lines that hold great ships to the shore.
To stop a sailing vessel by backing some sails while keeping others set. The ship drifts slowly, riding out a storm.
To move a ship by dropping a small anchor ahead and winching toward it. Laborious progress when wind fails.
The central structural beam running the length of the hull's bottom. The ship's spine. 'On an even keel' means balanced.
One nautical mile per hour. Measured by counting knots on a line paid out behind the ship—hence the name.
A short rope for securing or fastening. Now any cord worn around the neck—the sailor's reach extended to land.
The side sheltered from the wind. 'In the lee of' means protected by. The safe side of any obstacle.
A ship's tilt to one side from uneven loading or damage. Not rolling (temporary) but listing (persistent imbalance).
The official record of a ship's voyage. Named for the log thrown overboard to measure speed. Every captain's diary.
The arrangement by which a ship is secured in place—anchors, lines, buoys. A ship at rest is still held by many forces.
Markings on a ship's hull showing maximum safe loading depths for different water conditions. Samuel Plimsoll's lifesaving reform.
Rope rungs tied between shrouds, forming a ladder to climb the mast. Pronounced 'RAT-lins'. The sailor's stairway to heaven.
The system of ropes, cables, and chains supporting masts and controlling sails. Standing rigging stays; running rigging moves.
An opening in the ship's side to drain water from the deck. Also slang for to sink or ruin—scupper a plan.
A rope controlling a sail's angle to the wind. Not the sail itself—that's a common landlubber error.
Standing rigging that supports the mast from the sides. The mast's guy-wires, keeping it upright against the wind's push.
Measuring water depth with a weighted line. The leadsman's call—'by the mark, twain'—named Mark Twain.
To join ropes by interweaving their strands. 'Splice the mainbrace' meant an extra rum ration—celebration.
A large balloon-like sail used when running before the wind. Colorful and dramatic—the sail of speed and spectacle.
A strong rope supporting the mast from fore or aft. The forestay runs to the bow; the backstay to the stern.
The rear of the ship. Opposite of bow. Where the name is painted and the rudder hangs.
A continuous line of planking running the length of the hull. Ships are built strake by strake, plank over plank.
To turn the bow through the wind to change course. Also the course itself—on the port tack, on the starboard tack.
A seat across a boat, also serving as structural bracing. To sit athwart is to sit crosswise.
The sides of the hull above the waterline. What you paint, what people see, what takes the weather.
The flat surface at the stern. The ship's back wall—where the name is mounted, where the dinghy hangs.
The fore-and-aft balance of a ship in the water. Down by the bow or down by the stern—both problematic.
To raise the anchor preparatory to sailing. The moment of commitment—once weighed, you're going somewhere.
A horizontal rotating machine for raising the anchor. The capstan's horizontal cousin.
The outer end of a yard (horizontal spar). 'Sun over the yardarm' meant noon—time for the first drink.

Quod erat demonstrandum — that which was to be demonstrated. The triumphant conclusion of a proof, signaling the argument is complete. Euclid's mic drop. Now often replaced by a square (∎) or nothing at all.
terms.etymology: Latin: quod (which) + erat (was) + demonstrandum (to be demonstrated)

terms.definition: Own value — the scalar by which a linear transformation stretches its eigenvector. The special directions that don't rotate, only scale. Principal components in data. Resonant frequencies of systems. Quantum observables. The math is dry; the applications are everywhere.
terms.etymology: German: eigen (own, characteristic) + English value

terms.definition: Caused by medical treatment — the infection caught in hospital, the side effect worse than the disease. Medicine's dark side. First, do no harm is aspirational, not descriptive.
terms.etymology: Greek: iatros (healer) + genesis (origin)

terms.definition: Hospital-acquired — infections contracted during hospitalization. C. diff, MRSA, the bugs that breed where the sick gather. The paradox that hospitals can make you sicker.
terms.etymology: Greek: nosokomeion (hospital)

terms.definition: The study of causes — specifically, the cause of a disease. Unknown etiology: we don't know why this happens. The question before treatment: what went wrong?
terms.etymology: Greek: aitia (cause) + logos (study)

terms.definition: The predicted course of a disease — the forecast, the odds. Good prognosis: likely recovery. Poor prognosis: prepare affairs. The doctor's crystal ball, clouded by uncertainty.
terms.etymology: Greek: pro (before) + gnosis (knowledge)

terms.definition: The presence of multiple diseases simultaneously — diabetes and heart disease, depression and anxiety. Conditions cluster. Treatment complicates. The body doesn't respect diagnostic categories.
Treatment that relieves symptoms without curing — comfort care when cure fails. Pain management, quality of life. Not giving up but changing goals. The medicine of dignity.
terms.etymology: Latin: palliare (to cloak)

terms.definition: A treatment with no active ingredient that works anyway — the sugar pill that heals through belief. The placebo effect: 30-40% of drug efficacy. The mind-body problem made clinical.
terms.etymology: Latin: I shall please

terms.definition: Negative effects from expecting harm — the placebo's evil twin. Read the side effects and experience them. Voodoo death. Expectation shapes physiology.
terms.etymology: Latin: I shall harm

terms.definition: A sign or symptom so characteristic that it confirms diagnosis — Koplik's spots mean measles, no other tests needed. The diagnostic slam dunk. Rare in medicine; most symptoms are nonspecific.
Early symptoms before full disease — the aura before migraine, the fatigue before flu. The warning period. Sometimes actionable; often just ominous.
terms.etymology: Greek: pro (before) + dromos (running)

terms.definition: Of unknown cause — medicine's honest admission of ignorance. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: your lungs are scarring and we don't know why. The word that means 'we don't know.'
terms.etymology: Greek: idios (one's own) + pathos (suffering)

terms.definition: A condition resulting from a previous disease — the lung damage after COVID, the heart problems after rheumatic fever. The shadow the illness leaves. Recovery isn't always complete.

Leading motif — a recurring musical theme associated with a person, idea, or situation. Wagner's innovation: the ring, the sword, fate itself gets a melody. Now ubiquitous: Darth Vader's breath, Jaws' two notes.
terms.etymology: German: Leit (leading) + Motiv (motif)

terms.definition: Stolen time — expressive flexibility in tempo, borrowing time from one note to give to another. Romantic piano's heartbeat. Chopin's specialty. Not chaos but controlled spontaneity. The performer breathes.
terms.etymology: Italian: rubare (to steal)

terms.definition: Forcing — a sudden, strong accent on a single note. Abbreviated sfz. Beethoven's hammer blow. The unexpected emphasis that jolts attention.
terms.etymology: Italian: sforzare (to force)

terms.definition: Detached — notes played short and separated, the opposite of legato. Crisp, pointed articulation. Rain on a window. The space between notes matters as much as the notes.
terms.etymology: Italian: staccare (to detach)

terms.definition: Bound together — smooth, connected playing with no gaps between notes. The singing line. One breath from first note to last. The opposite of staccato.
terms.etymology: Italian: legare (to tie)

terms.definition: Growing — gradually increasing in volume. Ravel's Boléro is one long crescendo. Often misused to mean 'climax' but actually means the building, not the peak.
terms.etymology: Italian: crescere (to grow)

terms.definition: Diminishing — gradually decreasing in volume. The fade to silence. Also called decrescendo. Music returning to nothing.
terms.etymology: Italian: diminuire (to diminish)

terms.definition: Very soft — the quietest standard dynamic marking (pp). A whisper that demands attention. Harder than loud: control required.
Very loud — the loudest standard dynamic marking (ff). Full force, maximum power. Tchaikovsky's cannon fire. The orchestra's roar.
Vibrating — slight, rapid variation in pitch that warms and humanizes a note. String players' left hand, singers' throat. Too much is wobble; too little is dead. The voice's life.
Trembling — rapid repetition of a single note or alternation between two notes. String sections' shimmering curtain. Guitar's surf sound. Agitation made audible.
Sliding — continuous sweep between two notes, hitting every pitch between. Harp's cinematic swoop. Trombone's slide. The journey, not just departure and arrival.
Carrying — smooth glide between notes, more subtle than glissando. The voice's natural tendency. Pavarotti's trademark. Slide without showing the ladder.
terms.etymology: Italian: portare (to carry)

terms.definition: Plucked — string instruments plucked with fingers rather than bowed. Crisp, percussive, pointillistic. Delibes' pizzicato fairies. The violin pretending to be a harp.
terms.etymology: Italian: pizzicare (to pluck, pinch)

terms.definition: Bow — string instruments played with the bow after a pizzicato passage. The return to sustained tone. Resume normal operations.
With the wood — striking strings with the wooden back of the bow. Eerie, percussive, skeletal. Saint-Saëns' dancing bones. Holst's Mars. Violence to the instrument.
With mute — a device that dampens and veils the sound. Muted strings, muted brass: distant, ghostly, intimate. The voice heard through walls.
Obstinate — a repeated musical phrase, often in the bass. The ground that everything else dances over. Ravel's Boléro. Minimalism's foundation. Repetition as hypnosis.
terms.etymology: Italian: obstinate, persistent

terms.definition: Continuous bass — the Baroque accompaniment: bass line plus improvised chords, usually harpsichord and cello. The harmonic foundation that everyone builds on. Baroque's rhythm section.
From the head — go back to the beginning. D.C. al Fine: repeat from start until 'Fine' (end). Music's rewind button. The return that isn't quite repetition.
Tail — the concluding section of a piece, after the main structure. The goodbye, the final gesture. Beethoven's codas grew into second developments. The end that keeps ending.
Stop — a held note or rest, sustained beyond its written duration at performer's discretion. Time suspended. The breath before resolution. How long? As long as necessary.
Cadence — the virtuoso solo passage near the end of a concerto movement. The orchestra stops; the soloist flies alone. Originally improvised, now often composed. The moment of glory.
All — the full ensemble playing together, as opposed to solo sections. The orchestra's full force. Everyone in. The contrast that makes solos solos.
Filling — the full orchestra in a Baroque concerto grosso, contrasting with the concertino (small group of soloists). The backup singers to the concertino's stars.
Obligatory — an essential instrumental part, not optional accompaniment. The violin obbligato that can't be cut. Ironically, now often means 'optional.' Language drifts.
Beautiful singing — the Italian operatic style emphasizing pure, flowing tone and virtuoso ornamentation. Rossini, Bellini, Donizetti. Voice as instrument before drama mattered. Beauty first.
Coloring — elaborate ornamentation, particularly florid vocal runs and trills. Also: the soprano who sings such passages. The Queen of the Night's stratospheric fury.
Recited — speech-like singing that advances opera's plot between arias. Rhythm follows text, not meter. The connective tissue. What happens between the hits.
Air — a self-contained operatic song for solo voice with orchestra. The emotional pause where character reveals feeling. Plot stops; soul speaks. The bit you hum.
Texture — the range where a vocal part sits most of the time, regardless of highest and lowest notes. High tessitura exhausts even if no note is extreme. Where you live, not where you visit.
Passage — the transitional zone between vocal registers. Where the voice breaks if untrained. The bridge a singer must learn to cross smoothly. Yodeling exploits it; opera hides it.
Leaning note — a dissonant ornamental note that resolves by step. The tension before release. Mozart's signature weeping sound. The sigh made musical.
terms.etymology: Italian: appoggiare (to lean)

terms.definition: Crushed note — a very short grace note, played almost simultaneously with the main note and released immediately. The quick jab before the punch. Written with a slash through the stem.
terms.etymology: Italian: acciaccare (to crush)

terms.definition: Biting — a rapid alternation between a note and its lower neighbor. Quick, sharp ornament. The trill's shorter, punchier cousin. Baroque keyboard's fingerprint.
terms.etymology: From Latin mordere (to bite)

terms.definition: Chapel master — the director of music at a court or church. Bach's job title. Now sometimes pejorative: competent but uninspired, workmanlike. The steady professional.
Speaking voice — vocal technique between singing and speaking. Schoenberg's Pierrot Lunaire. Pitches indicated but not held. The uncanny valley of vocalization.
Tone-color melody — melody created by changes in timbre rather than pitch. Schoenberg's idea. A note passed between instruments becomes motion. Color as line.
Through-composed — music without repeated sections, continuously developing. The opposite of strophic songs. Schubert's Erlkönig: narrative demands no repetition. Each moment unique.
Upbeat — the anacrusis, the pickup note(s) before the first strong beat. The inhalation before the phrase. Also: conductor's preparatory gesture. Beginning before the beginning.
After-beat — ornamental notes following a main note or trill. The release after tension. What happens when the trill stops. The tail of the ornament.
A melodic framework for improvisation, with specific ascending/descending patterns, characteristic phrases, and emotional associations (rasa).
A rhythmic cycle that provides the temporal framework for composition and improvisation. Cycles range from 3 to 128 beats.
The smallest interval of pitch recognized in Indian music—22 shrutis per octave versus Western music's 12 semitones.
Ornamental techniques including oscillations, slides, and grace notes that give Indian classical music its distinctive expressiveness.
The slow, meditative, rhythm-free opening of a raga performance. The musician gradually reveals the raga's character, note by note.
A duet between two soloists, often playing different instruments. Competitive yet collaborative—musical dialogue and friendly combat.
A lineage or school of musicians passing down distinctive style through generations. Literally 'household'—musical knowledge as family inheritance.
The art of combining independent melodic lines. Point against point. Bach's supreme mastery.
A contrapuntal composition where voices enter successively with the same theme. Flight and pursuit.
A melody imitated exactly by another voice at a fixed interval. 'Row, Row, Row Your Boat.'
In a fugue, entries of the subject overlapping before previous entries finish. Intensification.
A sustained bass note over which harmonies change. The organist's feet hold steady.
Numbers below a bass line indicating chords to be improvised. Baroque shorthand.
Another term for basso continuo. The bass that runs through.
A recurring orchestral passage in Baroque concertos. The return.
A broken chord: notes played in succession rather than simultaneously.
At a walking pace. A moderate tempo.
Fast and lively. Literally 'cheerful.'
Slow and stately. 'At ease.'
Very fast. As fast as you can.
Stolen time: expressive flexibility with tempo. Chopin's specialty.
Exposition, development, recapitulation. The architecture of Classical first movements.
A form where the main theme keeps returning: ABACADA... The round.
A theme followed by modified versions. Identity through transformation.
A lively movement in triple time. 'Joke'—replaced the minuet in symphonies.
A stately dance in triple time. Standard movement in Classical symphonies.
Music without a tonal center. Schoenberg's liberation from keys.
Serialism using all twelve chromatic pitches in a fixed order. Schoenberg's method.
Organizing music by ordered series—of pitches, rhythms, dynamics. Post-war total organization.
Music incorporating chance: random elements, performer choice. Cage's dice.
Music made from recorded sounds, manipulated and assembled. Pierre Schaeffer's revolution.
Pared-down music: repetitive patterns, gradual change. Reich, Glass, Riley.
Music based on the acoustic properties of sound—overtones, spectra. French movement.
Arabic melodic mode: scales, characteristic phrases, emotional affect. The modal system of the Arab world.
Arabic instrumental improvisation exploring a maqam. Virtuosic, meditative.
An Arabic instrumental form in 10/8 time. Rhythmic complexity.
The fretless short-necked lute. Ancestor of the European lute. The sultan of instruments.
The modal system of Persian classical music. Twelve dastgahs, each a universe.
A melodic unit within a Persian dastgah. The building blocks of improvisation.
A long-necked Persian lute with figure-eight body. The instrument of dastgah.
Persian hammered dulcimer. Ancestor of the piano.
Rhythmic modes in Turkish classical music. Complex cycles, sometimes very long.
Turkish melodic modes, related to Arabic maqam but with distinct scales and practices.
Indonesian ensemble of bronze percussion. Interlocking patterns, shimmering sound. Bali, Java.
A five-note Javanese scale with roughly equal intervals.
A seven-note Javanese scale with unequal intervals.
Rhythmic structure marked by gong strokes. Indonesian ensemble organization.
Balinese interlocking rhythms: two parts combining into one rapid melody.
Korean narrative singing: one singer, one drummer. Hours-long epic dramas.
Korean solo instrumental form with drum accompaniment. Gradual acceleration.
Ancient Japanese court music. Solemn, slow, otherworldly.
Traditional Japanese music, as opposed to Western (yōgaku).
Japanese chamber music for koto, shamisen, and voice. Refined, intimate.
Japanese bamboo flute. Zen breathing meditation made sound.
Japanese thirteen-string zither. The sound of traditional Japan.
Japanese three-string lute. Kabuki, geisha, folk music.
Chinese seven-string zither. The scholar's instrument. Confucius played qin.
Chinese two-string bowed instrument. The voice of Chinese opera.
Chinese four-string lute. Virtuosic, expressive, ancient.
The small two-string fiddle of Beijing opera. Piercing, dramatic.
South Indian classical music. Ragas, talas, devotional. Tyagaraja's tradition.
North Indian classical music. Ragas, Persian influence, gharanas.
North Indian long-necked lute with sympathetic strings. Ravi Shankar's instrument.
North Indian hand drums: a pair with different pitches. Rhythmic virtuosity.
South Indian plucked string instrument. Saraswati's instrument.
South Indian barrel drum. The rhythmic anchor of Carnatic music.
The drone instrument of Indian classical music. The infinite hum beneath the raga.
West African hereditary musician and oral historian. The living library.
West African goblet drum. Goatskin, wood, hands. Global rhythm.
West African 21-string harp-lute. The griot's instrument.
West African wooden xylophone with gourd resonators.
Zimbabwean thumb piano: metal tines on a wooden board. Shona ancestral music.
Portuguese urban folk song. Longing, fate, saudade made audible.
Andalusian art: cante (song), toque (guitar), baile (dance). Gypsy passion.
'Deep song': the oldest, most profound style of flamenco singing.
Mexican folk ensemble: violins, guitars, trumpet. Serenade and celebration.
Afro-Mexican music from Veracruz. Jaranas, requinto, zapateado.
Argentine music and dance born in Buenos Aires. Bandoneon, melancholy, embrace.
The German concertina that became the voice of tango.
Brazilian music of African origin. Syncopation, drums, carnival.
'New trend': Brazilian music mixing samba with cool jazz. Jobim, Gilberto.
Brazilian instrumental genre: virtuosic, improvisatory, joyful weeping.
Brazilian Northeastern music: accordion, triangle, zabumba drum.
Traditional Ashkenazi Jewish music. Clarinet, violin, celebration and lament.
Hasidic wordless melody. The soul speaks without language.
Greek urban blues: bouzouki, underworld themes. The music of outcasts.
Producing multiple pitches simultaneously. Tuvan khoomei, Inuit katajjaq.
Tuvan/Mongolian throat singing. Overtones ring above the fundamental.
Mongolian horsehead fiddle. The sound of the steppe.
Australian Aboriginal drone instrument. Circular breathing, ancient earth.
Japanese drums, especially the large barrel drums played in ensemble.
Triangular Russian stringed instrument. Folk music's jangle.
Russian chromatic button accordion. Named for a legendary bard.
A stately Polish processional dance in triple time. National dignity in motion.
A Polish folk dance with accent on weak beats. Chopin wrote 58.
A fast Polish folk dance from the Kraków region.
A fast Polish folk dance with spinning couples.
A lively Bohemian dance in duple time. The Czech gift to world dance.
The river, the nation—Smetana's tone poem. Czech musical nationalism.
Bosnian blues: love-longing music with Ottoman roots. Bittersweet ache.
South Slavic single-string bowed instrument. Epic poetry sung to its drone.
South Slavic circle dance. Hands joined, feet flying.
Croatian/Serbian small long-necked lute. The sound of Slavonian parties.
Croatian a cappella singing, especially in Dalmatia. Male voices, harmony, emotion.
Bulgarian bowed string instrument. The sound of Bulgarian folk music.
Bulgarian bagpipe. Drone and chanter, the voice of the mountains.
Bulgarian folk dance in complex asymmetric meters. 7/8, 11/8—Balkan math.
Bulgarian folk dance in 7/8 time. The national dance.
Ukrainian plucked string instrument with many strings. Kobzar's companion.
Ukrainian traveling minstrel, often blind. Keeper of epic songs.
Ukrainian Cossack dance with spectacular leaps and squatting kicks.
Ancient Slavic plucked string instrument. The bard's harp.
The single-string bow that leads capoeira. Its rhythm sets the game.
The vast Hungarian steppe; also the emotional state of emptiness and wild freedom it evokes—a landscape that is both desolate and liberating.
The feeling of solitude and connectedness to nature when alone in the woods. A specifically German form of forest contemplation.
terms.etymology: From Wald (forest) + Einsamkeit (solitude)

terms.definition: The reflection of moonlight on water; the shimmering path the moon makes on the sea at night.
Lightning; also electricity. The spark that illuminates and transforms—a metaphor for sudden insight.
Sunlight filtering through leaves; the interplay of light and shadow when sun shines through a canopy of trees.
terms.etymology: From 木 (ko, tree) + 漏れ (more, leaking) + 日 (bi, sun)

terms.definition: Refined conduct, literary culture, the ethics of comportment. In classical Arabic usage: the body of knowledge and behaviour expected of a cultivated person — proper manners, command of poetry, historical learning, controlled emotion. In Persian court culture: the entire civilisational complex of letters, etiquette, and aesthetic refinement. The adīb (man of adab) is the Islamic humanist. The concept has no single Western equivalent: it is simultaneously Bildung, courtesy, and literary canon.
terms.etymology: Arabic root أ-د-ب (ʾ-d-b): to discipline, to invite to a banquet. The sense expanded from table manners to all of culture.

terms.definition: Struggle, contest — the principle of organised conflict that the Greeks considered essential to excellence. The Olympic Games, the tragic festival, the law court, the philosophical dialogue: all are agōnes. Nietzsche's Homer's Contest argues that Greek culture was built on the agonistic impulse — the excellence-generating rivalry that required worthy opponents. Without the agōn, culture does not simply become peaceful; it becomes mediocre.
terms.etymology: Greek: contest, struggle. Root of agony, protagonist, antagonist.

terms.definition: Non-harming. The ethical principle central to Jainism, Buddhism, and Hinduism: the refusal to cause harm to any living being. In Jainism, the absolute principle. In Gandhi's political programme, transformed into a technique of resistance: ahiṃsā not as passivity but as the most demanding form of action — requiring more courage than violence because it refuses the easy exit of retaliation.
terms.etymology: A- (non-) + hiṃsā (harm, violence), from the root han (to strike). First appears in the Chandogya Upanishad.

terms.definition: Truth as unconcealment. Not correctness (a statement matching a fact) but disclosure — the showing-forth of what was hidden. Heidegger's reading: truth is not a property of propositions but an event of unconcealment. The river shows what was always there. The etymology matters: a-letheia, the un-forgotten.
terms.etymology: A- (un-) + lethe (forgetting, concealment). Lethe is the river of forgetfulness in Hades.

terms.definition: Love of fate; the attitude of not merely accepting but embracing everything that happens, including suffering and loss.
terms.etymology: Amor (love) + fati (of fate)
terms.usage: Nietzsche advocated amor fati as the highest formula of affirmation.

terms.definition: Contentment with one's lot; accepting one's fate with peace rather than striving for more.

The analogy of being. The Catholic metaphysical claim that creation participates in God's being without being identical to it — beings are neither wholly different from God (equivocal) nor the same (univocal) but analogous. The analogia entis makes natural theology possible: we can reason from the world toward God because they share a proportional relationship. Karl Barth called it 'the invention of the Antichrist' — the attempt to reach God by human reason rather than revelation. The debate between Barth and Przywara defines 20th-century theology.
