Sufi devotional songs in Urdu/Punjabi. Ecstatic, repetitive, transcendent.
An Urdu poetry gathering where poets recite and audiences respond. Living literary tradition.
African oral poetry praising chiefs, ancestors, or animals. Izibongo (Zulu), oriki (Yoruba).
Zulu praise poetry. Performed at ceremonies, praising kings and ancestors.
Yoruba praise poetry. Names and epithets invoking personal and family history.
Visual poetry where typography and arrangement are meaning. The poem as image.
Poetry made from existing text: newspapers, manuals, overheard speech. Reframing as art.
Poetry created by erasing words from an existing text, leaving a new poem.
Internet-age poetry: deliberately bad, absurdist, using Google search results. Anti-aesthetic.
Avant-garde American poetry foregrounding language itself. Disjunction, fragmentation.
Early 20th-century movement: direct treatment, no excess words, musical rhythm. Pound, H.D., Williams.
1930s movement emphasizing sincerity and objectification. Zukofsky, Oppen, Reznikoff.
Personal, autobiographical poetry. Lowell, Plath, Sexton. The private made public.
Poetry drawing on the unconscious for images. Bly, Wright. Surrealism Americanized.
Poetry from Black Mountain College: projective verse, open form. Olson, Creeley, Duncan.
Olson's theory: breath-based composition, the typewriter as scoring device. Open field.
Poets connected to Abstract Expressionism: playful, urban, anti-academic. O'Hara, Ashbery, Koch.
Countercultural poetry of the 1950s-60s. Ginsberg's Howl, spontaneous prosody. 'I saw the best minds...'
Ouvroir de Littérature Potentielle: constrained writing. Lipograms, prisoner's constraint. Perec, Queneau.
Writing that excludes one or more letters. Perec's La Disparition has no 'e.'
A poem where each line is an anagram of the title or previous line.
A poem where initial letters spell a word or message. Hidden signatures.
A poem where each line or stanza begins with successive letters of the alphabet.
A poem where end words, read down, form a line from another poem. Terrance Hayes invented it.
A poem made entirely of lines from other poems. Patchwork poetry. Ancient practice.
A poem or song using an existing melody or form with new words. Sacred made secular or vice versa.
Russian epic oral poetry celebrating bogatyrs (heroes). Sung, not recited.
A short Russian folk poem, often humorous or satirical. Sung rapidly, four lines.
Ukrainian epic song of Cossack deeds. Sung by kobzars.

State of exception. Carl Schmitt's concept in Political Theology (1922): "Sovereign is he who decides on the exception." The sovereign is defined not by normal governance but by the power to suspend the legal order in emergency — and thereby reveal that the legal order depends on a pre-legal decision. Agamben extended it: the state of exception has become the permanent paradigm of government in modernity. Guantánamo, emergency powers, indefinite detention — the exception has become the rule.
terms.etymology: Ausnahme (exception) + Zustand (state, condition). Political Theology: Vier Kapitel zur Lehre von der Souveränität, 1922.

quotes.text: Souverän ist, wer über den Ausnahmezustand entscheidet.
quotes.source: Carl Schmitt, Politische Theologie, 1922

terms.definition: Upheaval, overturning. A word that does more than 'revolution' — it carries the physical sensation of being turned upside down. The bouleversement is not only political but affective: a complete disorientation of the known order. French history is structured by them; the word has the weight of recurrence.
terms.etymology: From bouleverser — to overturn, from boule (ball) + verser (to pour, to turn).

terms.definition: An act or event that provokes or justifies war; the occasion for war.
terms.etymology: Casus (fall, occasion) + belli (of war)
terms.usage: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand provided the casus belli for World War I.

terms.definition: Destruction, catastrophe. Originally the destruction of the First Temple (586 BCE) and Second Temple (70 CE). Extended to the Holocaust — many Eastern European Jews initially called it the Churban rather than Shoah. The word carries the theology of destruction as rupture in the covenant, followed by mourning, and the possibility of return. A word that names not just destruction but its specific structure: the destruction of what was sacred.
terms.etymology: From the root ח-ר-ב (ḥ-r-b), meaning desolation, ruin. The same root as ḥorev (sword).

terms.definition: Condemnation of memory. The Roman practice of erasing a person from the historical record — removing inscriptions, melting statues, burning documents — as if they had never existed. A punishment beyond death. Soviet airbrushing, Twitter deplatforming, colonial statue-removal: all are damnatio memoriae, though only the Roman original was legally codified.
terms.etymology: Damnatio (condemnation, from damnare) + memoriae (genitive of memoria, memory).

terms.definition: The blood levy. The Ottoman practice of conscripting Christian boys — primarily from the Balkans — converting them to Islam and training them for elite military and administrative service as janissaries and palace officials. The system produced the empire's most loyal servants precisely because they had no other allegiance: no tribe, no family inheritance, no competing loyalty. Paradox: the empire's strength came from those it had uprooted. Many of its greatest grand viziers were devşirme boys.
terms.etymology: From devşirmek (to collect, to levy). The system operated c. 1380–1648.

terms.definition: Decisionism — the doctrine that the ultimate ground of political order is not reason, norm, or value but a pure decision. Schmitt's position: the legal order is not self-grounding; it rests on a primordial act of will that cannot be derived from anything else. The decision precedes the norm. This is both a political critique (liberalism's pretence of normative self-sufficiency) and a vulnerability (it makes power the ultimate reality). Weber's polytheism of values and Nietzsche's will to power are its philosophical relatives.
terms.etymology: From Latin decisio (decision, cutting through). Schmitt's term for the primacy of the will over the norm.

terms.definition: Hegemony — consent manufactured into domination. Gramsci's Prison Notebooks concept: the ruling class does not maintain power through force alone but through cultural leadership — making its worldview appear as common sense, natural, inevitable. Hegemony is the achievement of consent from the dominated. Counter-hegemony requires a "war of position" — the slow construction of alternative institutions, values, and intellectual leadership before any seizure of power. The concept transformed how the left thought about culture and ideology.
terms.etymology: From Greek hēgemonia (leadership, dominance). Gramsci distinguished it from domination (direct coercion).

quotes.text: The State is the entire complex of practical and theoretical activities with which the ruling class not only justifies and maintains its dominance, but manages to win the active consent of those over whom it rules.
quotes.source: Antonio Gramsci, Prison Notebooks

terms.definition: Divine glory, the luminous kingship aura. In Zoroastrian cosmology, the farr is the sign of legitimate sovereignty — visible radiance that attaches to righteous rulers and abandons tyrants the moment they transgress. When Jamshid became proud, the farr fled him in the form of a bird. It is not merely charisma but a cosmic verdict: the universe withdrawing its endorsement.
terms.etymology: Avestan xvarənah. The concept runs from the Avesta through the Shahnameh into Safavid and Mughal imperial ideology.

terms.definition: Civil strife, temptation, chaos. The most feared concept in Islamic political thought: the internal conflict that destroys the community. The early Muslim civil wars were fitna; so was the seduction to apostasy. The word unifies political disorder and spiritual temptation — both are forms of the same dissolution. Against fitna, even an unjust ruler was preferable to chaos.
terms.etymology: From fatana (to try, to tempt, to afflict). The root covers trial, sedition, and enchantment.

terms.definition: Making superficial changes to preserve the existing power structure; 'everything must change so that everything stays the same.'
terms.etymology: From 'Il Gattopardo' (The Leopard) by Lampedusa
terms.usage: The Risorgimento is often criticized as an exercise in gattopardismo.

terms.definition: Inner emigration. The practice of German writers and intellectuals who remained in Germany during the Nazi period but withdrew into private, coded, or historical subjects — neither actively collaborating nor actively resisting. Contested after 1945: was it complicity or survival? Thomas Mann attacked it from exile; Ernst Jünger embodied it from within.
terms.etymology: Coined to describe those who 'emigrated inward' rather than leaving the country.

terms.definition: The educated class with a conscience. The Russian term names not merely the educated but those who feel a moral obligation toward social transformation — the class that reads, debates, and believes it owes something to the people. Its defining tension: educated enough to see the problems, marginal enough to be unable to fix them. The word migrated westward as a general term but has never shed its Russian political charge.
terms.etymology: From Latin intelligentia (understanding). The Russian intelligentsia was theorised by Boborkykin in the 1860s.

terms.definition: The restrainer — the force that holds back the end of the world. Paul's 2 Thessalonians 2:6-7: "you know what is restraining him now." Schmitt applied it to political theology: the Holy Roman Empire as the katechon, the force that prevented the unleashing of the Antichrist. The concept names the conservative function of any empire or institution: its legitimacy rests not on justice but on restraint — the prevention of something worse. Every status quo power claims to be a katechon.
terms.etymology: Greek: present participle of katechein (to hold back, to restrain). From kata (down, against) + echein (to have, to hold).

terms.definition: I am the state; attributed to Louis XIV, expressing the absolute identification of monarch and nation.
terms.etymology: L'État (the state) + c'est (is) + moi (me)
terms.usage: Whether or not Louis XIV said it, the phrase captures the essence of absolutism.

terms.definition: The French doctrine of strict separation between religious institutions and the public sphere — more demanding than the Anglo-American concept of secularism. Not merely tolerance but the positive exclusion of religion from public life and state institutions. The 1905 law. The headscarf debates. A specifically French resolution of the Enlightenment's demand for universalism over particular identity.
terms.etymology: From laïc (layman, non-clerical), from Greek laos (people). The opposite is clérical.

terms.definition: The originary act of land-seizure that founds all law. Schmitt's concept in The Nomos of the Earth: before there can be law there must be a taking (Nahme) — the violent appropriation of land that establishes the spatial order within which norms become possible. International law rests on the jus publicum Europaeum — the European states' agreement about how to divide the rest of the world. In classical Greek, nomos meant both law and pasture — the distribution that is also a habitation.
terms.etymology: Greek nomos (law, custom, pasture). Schmitt's concept of Ur-Nahme (originary seizure) is deliberately etymological.

terms.definition: The reclamation of African identity and cultural value against assimilation. Aimé Césaire and Léopold Sédar Senghor's concept (1930s): the refusal of the colonial demand to become French, the affirmation of African culture, aesthetics, and history as sources of value rather than deficits to be overcome. The concept's internal tension: Senghor's version risked essentialising African identity; Sartre called it a "negative moment" in the dialectic that would be superseded. Fanon criticised it as a bourgeois nationalism that left colonial structures intact.
terms.etymology: Négritude: from nègre (the reclaimed slur) + -itude (abstract suffix). The act of reclaiming the insult is constitutive of the concept.

quotes.text: Ma négritude n'est pas une pierre, sa surdité ruée contre la clameur du jour.
quotes.source: Aimé Césaire, Cahier d'un retour au pays natal, 1939

terms.definition: Fearless speech. The obligation to speak truth to power, regardless of risk. Foucault's concept in his late lectures: the parrhesiastes (truth-teller) must be in a position of danger — speaking down to equals costs nothing. The Socratic obligation. The whistleblower's burden. A mode of speech that requires courage as its precondition.
terms.etymology: Pan- (all) + rhesis (speech). Complete speech — holding nothing back.

terms.definition: Fullness of power. The papal claim, developed by Innocent III and Innocent IV, that the pope holds absolute sovereign authority — spiritual and temporal — over the entire Christian world. The doctrine that produced the most extreme medieval claims to universal jurisdiction. Its theoretical limits were contested by canonists, bishops, and emperors for three centuries. The modern concept of sovereignty — absolute, indivisible, above law — is its secularised descendant.
terms.etymology: Plenitudo (fullness) + potestatis (genitive of potestas, power). First formulated by Pope Leo I (5th c.), systematised in the 13th.

terms.definition: Reason of state; the principle that the state's interest justifies any action, including those that would otherwise be immoral.
terms.etymology: Raison (reason) + d'état (of state)
terms.usage: Richelieu elevated raison d'état above religious considerations in French policy.

terms.definition: Politics based on practical and material factors rather than ideological or moral considerations; pragmatic power politics.
terms.etymology: Real (realistic) + Politik (politics)
terms.usage: Bismarck's Realpolitik unified Germany through calculated diplomacy and war.

terms.definition: Passive revolution — transformation without rupture. Gramsci's concept for political change managed from above to prevent change from below: the ruling class that incorporates enough of the revolutionary programme to defuse the revolutionary pressure. The Risorgimento was a passive revolution: national unification without the agrarian revolution that would have required the peasantry. Fascism was a passive revolution. Every managed reform that co-opts the radical demand while neutralising the radical movement is a rivoluzione passiva.
terms.etymology: Gramsci's term, derived from Cuoco's analysis of the failed Neapolitan revolution of 1799.

terms.definition: The Reorganisation. The Ottoman reform programme of 1839–1876 — a sustained attempt to modernise the empire's legal, administrative, and educational structures along European lines while preserving Ottoman sovereignty. The Gülhane Edict (1839) guaranteed rights to all subjects regardless of religion. The project's structural failure: reforms advanced enough to delegitimise the old order but not enough to replace it. Every late colonial modernisation is a Tanzimat.
terms.etymology: Arabic tanzīm (organisation, ordering) in Ottoman Turkish. The period is also called the Era of Tanzimat.

terms.definition: Comrade — the word that tried to replace all others. The Bolshevik address that abolished "mister," "master," and all titles of rank: everyone is a comrade. The concept carries the entire project of revolutionary equality in a single word of address. Its failure is also encoded in the word: the moment when "Comrade Stalin" became more terrifying than any title of the old regime, the word became its own opposite. The life and death of tovarishch is the history of the Soviet Union compressed into a term of address.
terms.etymology: From tovar (goods, trade). A tovarishch was originally a business partner or travelling companion — the revolutionary sense came through the labour movement.

terms.definition: The transfer of empire. The medieval doctrine that the Roman Empire had not ended but migrated — to Charlemagne, to the Holy Roman Empire, potentially to each new claimant of universal sovereignty. Power is not created ex nihilo; it is transmitted, inherited, transferred. The doctrine structured medieval political theology and underwrote every claim to universal authority. Every modern nationalism that claims to be the heir of an ancient civilisation is performing a translatio imperii.
terms.etymology: Translatio (transfer, translation) + imperii (genitive of imperium). Also translatio studii: the parallel transfer of learning.

terms.definition: Political opportunism; the practice of shifting alliances and co-opting opponents to maintain power, characteristic of Italian politics after unification.
terms.etymology: From 'trasformare' (to transform)
terms.usage: Depretis institutionalized trasformismo, blurring left-right distinctions.

terms.definition: Familyhood — Julius Nyerere's concept of African socialism. The Tanzanian ujamaa programme (1967–1977) attempted to build socialism on the basis of traditional African communal life: the extended family as the model for economic organisation, the village as the unit of production. The experiment's failure is as instructive as its ideals: ujamaa villagisation was partly coercive, and the identification of "traditional" with "socialist" suppressed both indigenous complexity and legitimate critique.
terms.etymology: Swahili: familyhood, kinship. From jamaa (family, community), from Arabic jamāʿah (group, congregation).

terms.definition: Primal catastrophe. Diplomat George Kennan's term for the First World War as the originary disaster of the twentieth century — the event from which all subsequent catastrophes (fascism, Stalinism, WWII, Cold War) derived. The word is German because German political thought needed a single term for the inaugural wound.
terms.etymology: Ur- (primal, original, archaic) + Katastrophe (catastrophe). The Ur- prefix appears in Urtext, Urform.

terms.definition: World-improver. The person who believes the world can and should be made better — used ironically in German for the naive idealist, more often than not. The word's ironic register is the key: German political culture is suspicious of abstract meliorism. Compare to the untranslated English faith in 'change-makers.'
terms.etymology: Welt (world) + verbessern (to improve) + -er (agent suffix).

terms.definition: Group solidarity, social cohesion. Ibn Khaldun's central concept in the Muqaddima (1377): the bond of loyalty and solidarity that gives a people — especially a tribe or dynasty — its capacity for conquest and political survival. ʿAsabiyya rises in the desert, is corrupted by urban luxury, declines, and the cycle begins again. The first sociological theory of history.
terms.etymology: From ʿasaba (to bind). The bond is simultaneously kinship, loyalty, and collective identity.

terms.definition: The state in which — the existing condition. Defending the status quo versus demanding change. Often pejorative now: complacency, inertia, protecting privilege.
Voice of the people — public opinion. Vox populi, vox dei: the voice of the people is the voice of God. Democratic legitimacy, or mob rule, depending on your politics.

Deng Xiaoping Theory — 'Socialism with Chinese characteristics,' the ideological framework for market reforms under Communist rule. It doesn't matter if the cat is black or white, as long as it catches mice. Pragmatism as doctrine.

One China Policy — the principle that there is only one China, with Taiwan as part of it. Both PRC and ROC officially agree (or agreed); they just disagree on who governs. The diplomatic fiction that prevents war while satisfying no one.

Heavenly sovereign — the Emperor of Japan, descendant of the sun goddess Amaterasu. Unbroken line for 2,600 years (mythologically). Divine until 1946, now constitutional symbol. Reigns but does not rule, except when he does.

National polity — the essence of Japan as a unique divine nation under the Emperor. State Shinto's core doctrine. What Japan fought WWII to preserve. The concept the postwar constitution carefully didn't abolish.
Descent from heaven — retired bureaucrats taking cushy jobs in industries they regulated. Legal corruption, revolving door, captured regulators. The career path that blurs public and private.
The village commune that collectively held land. Also means 'world' and 'peace'—all one word.
Restructuring: Gorbachev's 1980s reforms. Political and economic opening.
Openness, transparency. Gorbachev's policy of public disclosure.
The Soviet elite: party members holding key positions. The ruling class.
A Communist Party bureaucrat. The machine's functionary.
Self-published dissident literature, copied and passed hand to hand.
Dissident literature published abroad and smuggled back.
The Polish trade union that helped end communism. Workers' revolution.
A public square. The site of Ukraine's revolutions: Orange, Euromaidan.

The noon-day demon. The spiritual torpor that afflicts monks at midday — not laziness but the inability to care: a profound indifference to one's own salvation and to the world. Cassian and Evagrius Ponticus described it as the most dangerous of the eight passions because it mimics rest while being its opposite. Aquinas made it a capital sin. Cioran, Baudelaire, and the entire tradition of ennui are secular descendants. Agamben: acedia is the refusal to will one's own possibility.
terms.etymology: Latin from Greek akēdia: a- (without) + kēdos (care, grief). The medieval 'sloth' translation impoverishes the concept.

terms.definition: Acting out — repeating in action what cannot be remembered. Freud's concept: the patient who cannot recall a repressed memory will instead repeat it, compulsively enacting it in the present rather than making it conscious. The neurotic does not remember the primal scene; they re-live it in every relationship. Psychoanalytic treatment is the conversion of repetition into remembering. Politically: nations that cannot mourn their past act it out — Freud's own argument about post-WWI Germany.
terms.etymology: From Latin agere (to do, to act). Freud's German term; the English 'acting out' is the standard translation.

terms.definition: The spontaneous perception of connections and meaningfulness in unrelated things. Klaus Conrad coined it (1958) as a clinical term for early psychosis: the patient begins to find hidden significance everywhere — in licence plates, overheard conversations, the arrangement of objects. Extended by Philip K. Dick and conspiracy theory researchers: the pathology that underlies pattern-recognition, the capacity that makes both science and paranoia possible. The same cognitive machinery finds the signal and the noise.
terms.etymology: Greek apo (away from) + phaenein (to show). Conrad distinguished it from anaesthesia (the loss of meaning) — apophenia is its excess.

terms.definition: Reheated cabbage; the attempt to revive a failed relationship or project. Never as good as the original.

The Thing — the unrepresentable real object that desire circles without reaching. Freud's concept in Project for a Scientific Psychology, systematised by Lacan in Seminar VII: the Ethics of Psychoanalysis. Das Ding is not an object in the world but the void around which the world of objects is organised — the original lost object (the mother's body) whose loss constitutes desire. Art is the construction of a Thing — a beautiful object that surrounds the void without filling it.
terms.etymology: German: the thing. Distinguished from das Objekt (the object of desire, which is always a substitute).

terms.definition: Far-pain. The longing for distant places — the opposite of Heimweh (homesickness). Where Heimweh aches for what you have left, Fernweh aches for places you have never been. The traveller's disease. The world is always more interesting elsewhere.
terms.etymology: Fern (far, distant) + Weh (pain, ache). Structurally parallel to Heimweh.

terms.definition: Fingertip feeling; instinctive sensitivity and tact. The ability to handle delicate situations with subtlety.

Gone/Here. Freud's observation in Beyond the Pleasure Principle: his 18-month-old grandson threw a spool out of his cot (fort — gone) and pulled it back (da — here), repeatedly. Freud read it as the child's mastery of the mother's absence — turning passive suffering into active play, instituting representation. The origin of language, of the symbol, of culture: the capacity to make present what is absent. Lacan: the fort/da is the entry into the symbolic order — the subject is constituted in the moment they can say 'gone.'
terms.etymology: German fort (away, gone) and da (there, here). The episode is in Jenseits des Lustprinzips (1920).

terms.definition: Someone who wears gloves to throw snowballs; a coward who criticizes from safety.

The collective melancholy of Istanbul. Orhan Pamuk's concept in Istanbul: Memories and the City — distinguished from individual sadness, from German Trauer, from Portuguese saudade. Hüzün is the shared mood of a city mourning its own imperial decline: the peeling plaster of wooden yalıs, the Bosphorus in winter mist, the consciousness of having once been the centre of the world. It is not depression but a form of pride — the melancholy of those who carry a great past in a diminished present.
terms.etymology: From Arabic ḥuzn (sadness). The Turkish word acquired its collective, civilisational dimension through Pamuk's theorisation.

terms.definition: Shadow, shade; also dignity, presence, gravitas. The weight of personhood one carries.

Enjoyment that exceeds and undermines pleasure. Lacan's technical term — distinguished from plaisir (pleasure, the release of tension): jouissance is the enjoyment that hurts, the compulsive repetition beyond the pleasure principle. It is what keeps the subject returning to what damages them. Translated inadequately as 'enjoyment' or left untranslated. Politically: Žižek argues that ideology operates not through ideas but through the jouissance attached to cultural practices — what we enjoy in our way of life.
terms.etymology: French verb jouir (to enjoy, to come) + -ance. The word spans enjoyment, orgasm, and legal possession (jouissance of property).

terms.definition: Head cinema; the vivid mental images or scenarios that play in your mind, especially when imagining possibilities or reliving memories.
terms.etymology: From Kopf (head) + Kino (cinema)

terms.definition: Air castle; a pipe dream or unrealistic fantasy. Castles built in the air rather than on solid ground.
terms.etymology: From Luft (air) + Schloss (castle)

terms.definition: Deferred action, afterwardness. Freud's concept that trauma does not operate at the moment of occurrence but is constituted retroactively — a later event rewrites the earlier one, giving it its traumatic meaning. The past is not fixed; it is continuously revised by the present. Lacan emphasised it: the subject's history is not what happened but what is constructed from what happened. The concept dissolves the linear model of cause and effect in psychic life.
terms.etymology: Nach (after) + träglich (from tragen, to carry). The sense: that which is carried after, or which comes to bear afterward. Laplanche and Pontalis introduced it to English as 'afterwardness.'

terms.definition: The place where one feels most oneself. From bullfighting: the spot in the ring where the bull returns for safety — from which it fights with most authority and confidence. Extended: the space, place, or activity from which a person draws their deepest sense of self. Not nostalgia but a present-tense orientation.
terms.etymology: From querer (to love, to want). The querencia is the loved place.

terms.definition: Pleasure derived from another person's misfortune.
terms.etymology: Schaden (damage, harm) + Freude (joy)
terms.usage: Nietzsche analyzed Schadenfreude as a manifestation of ressentiment.

terms.definition: Extraordinary determination and courage in adversity; Finnish grit. The strength to keep going when all seems lost.
Sitting flesh; the ability to sit through tedious tasks with endurance. Buttocks as metaphor for patience.

Solitude that aches. Not simply aloneness — soledad is inhabited, productive, sorrowful. The solitude of the flamenco singer, the desert mystic, the exile. Machado (Antonio): 'caminante, son tus huellas el camino y nada más.' The concept is embedded in Spanish Romanticism and the Generation of '98's diagnosis of Spain's historical isolation.
terms.etymology: From Latin solitudo (solitude). The suffix -edad intensifies into a condition, not merely a state.

terms.definition: The redirection of sexual and aggressive drives toward culturally valued ends. Freud's concept: civilisation is built on the sublimation of drives — art, science, and philosophy are forms of redirected libidinal energy. Leonardo's painting is sublimated sexuality. The concept is simultaneously flattering (art is powerful) and deflating (art is substitute). Lacan refined it: sublimation raises an object to the dignity of the Thing — it does not redirect the drive but transforms its aim.
terms.etymology: From Latin sublimare (to elevate, to lift up). Chemical term: solid directly to vapour without liquid phase — Freud used the analogy deliberately.

terms.definition: Gate-closing panic. The anxiety that time is running out — that a gate is closing and you will be left outside. Used especially for the fear of missed life milestones: marriage, children, career achievement. The medievally-literal German encodes an entire psychology of foreclosure.
terms.etymology: Tor (gate) + Schluss (closing) + Panik (panic). The closing gate of a walled city before nightfall.

terms.definition: Anguished longing with nowhere to go. Nabokov: 'No single word in English renders all the shades of toska. At its deepest and most painful, it is a sensation of great spiritual anguish, often without any specific cause. At less morbid levels it is a dull ache of the soul, a longing with nothing to long for.' Toska is Weltschmerz without the idealism — pure ache.
terms.etymology: Old Slavic. Related to tesnota (tightness, constriction) — the sensation of being pressed.

terms.definition: The uncanny valley. Masahiro Mori's 1970 concept: as a robot's appearance approaches human likeness, our affinity increases — until it gets very close, at which point it plunges into revulsion, then recovers only at perfect likeness. The valley is the interval where almost-human is more disturbing than obviously-not-human. Freud's Unheimliche is its theoretical explanation: the familiar made strange triggers the return of repressed anxieties about the boundaries of the self.
terms.etymology: Mori's original Japanese: 不気味の谷 (bukimi no tani). The German framing connects it explicitly to Freud.

terms.definition: The compulsion to travel. More than curiosity — an ache, a drive that cannot be satisfied by staying still. The Romantic walker who must keep moving to feel alive. Borrowed wholesale into English because English has no equivalent for the compulsive dimension: wandering as psychological necessity.
terms.etymology: wandern (to hike, to travel) + Lust (desire, pleasure). The German Romantic walking tradition.

terms.definition: The compulsion to repeat. Freud's concept in Beyond the Pleasure Principle: the tendency to re-enact painful experiences, to return to damaging relationships, to reproduce what hurt rather than what pleased. It led Freud to posit the death drive (Todestrieb) — a force in the organism working against life, toward the return to an earlier inorganic state. The concept exceeds clinical psychology: every historical cycle, every return to war, every nation that cannot stop rehearsing its traumas is in the grip of Wiederholungszwang.
terms.etymology: Wiederholung (repetition) + Zwang (compulsion). Introduced in Jenseits des Lustprinzips, 1920.

terms.definition: Bravery, gallantry, and manly virtue; courage with style and honor.
Love of honor; the complex of virtues including pride, dignity, generosity, and doing right by others. The essence of Greek character.
terms.etymology: From φίλος (filos, friend/love) + τιμή (timi, honor)

terms.definition: Stubborn defiance out of spite; doing something difficult or unreasonable purely to prove a point, even against one's own interest.
terms.etymology: From Turkish inat (stubbornness)

terms.definition: Measured, moderate, temperate; having an inner equilibrium that manifests in calm, balanced behavior and aesthetic restraint.
Water of the heart; generosity, kindness, and thoughtfulness. The flow of goodwill between people.
Cool heart; staying calm and composed. The opposite of jai rawn (hot heart). Essential Thai virtue.
Enduring the seemingly unbearable with patience and dignity; stoic perseverance through hardship without complaint.
Earnest, serious, diligent; someone who takes responsibilities seriously. A core Japanese virtue.

Choosing an option that's good enough rather than optimal — Herbert Simon's portmanteau of satisfy and suffice. Bounded rationality: we can't maximize, so we accept the first acceptable choice. Not laziness but realistic. Often better than exhaustive search.
In wine, truth — alcohol loosens tongues, reveals character. Pliny's observation. The drunk speaks what the sober thinks. Hence strategic inebriation in negotiation.

The mental discomfort of holding contradictory beliefs — the smoker who knows smoking kills. We resolve it by changing beliefs, adding rationalizations, or ignoring information. Festinger's discovery: the mind demands consistency.

The cognitive bias where incompetent people overestimate their ability while experts underestimate theirs — you need competence to recognize incompetence. The confidence of the ignorant. Mount Stupid before the valley of despair.

The tendency to seek and interpret information that confirms existing beliefs — we google to prove ourselves right, not to learn. The algorithm of self-reinforcement. The bias that makes all other biases sticky.

Over-relying on the first piece of information encountered — the initial price sets expectations, the first number frames negotiation. Arbitrary anchors affect judges, doctors, everyone. The power of going first.

Judging probability by how easily examples come to mind — plane crashes feel more common than car accidents because they're memorable. Vivid beats statistical. The news distorts reality by selecting the dramatic.

Continuing a losing course because of past investment — the movie is bad but you've paid for the ticket. Throwing good money after bad. The inability to write off what's already lost. Concorde fallacy.
Believing after the fact that you knew it all along — 'I knew the market would crash.' Memory rewrites itself. The obstacle to learning from mistakes. Everyone's a genius in hindsight.
Attributing others' behavior to character while attributing our own to circumstance — he's late because he's irresponsible; I'm late because of traffic. We're harsher judges of others than ourselves.

Letting one positive trait color perception of everything else — attractive people seem smarter, successful companies seem well-managed. The cognitive shortcut that distorts judgment. First impressions contaminate everything.
Giving up after repeated failure even when escape becomes possible — Seligman's dogs stopped trying. The psychological trap of depression and poverty. When trauma teaches that action is futile.

Manipulating someone into questioning their own reality — from the 1944 film where a husband dims gaslights while denying change. Psychological abuse through reality distortion. 'That never happened. You're crazy.'
Attributing your own unacceptable thoughts to others — the cheater who suspects cheating, the liar who trusts no one. Freudian defense mechanism. We see in others what we can't face in ourselves.
Redirecting feelings about one person onto another — the patient who falls in love with the therapist, seeing a parent. Freud's discovery, now therapeutic tool. The past animating the present.
Channeling unacceptable impulses into socially acceptable activities — aggression into sports, sexuality into art. The healthiest defense mechanism. Civilization built on redirected drives.

Learning through consequences — Skinner's rats pressing levers. Positive reinforcement, negative reinforcement, punishment. The behaviorist mechanism beneath all training. Reward what you want; ignore what you don't.

The brain's ability to rewire itself — forming new connections, reassigning functions. The discovery that ended 'hardwired' pessimism. Stroke patients recover; meditators change structure. The brain as ongoing construction site.
Inertia, apathy, inability to act. From Goncharov's character Oblomov, who can't get out of bed.
Suffering, dissatisfaction, unease; the First Noble Truth of Buddhism. Life's inherent unsatisfactoriness.
Inner fire; a meditation practice that generates intense internal heat. Tibetan monks can dry wet sheets on their bodies in freezing cold.
Hidden treasure; sacred texts or objects concealed by masters to be discovered when the time is right.
Sending and receiving; a meditation practice of breathing in others' suffering and breathing out compassion and relief.
In-between state; the transitional states between death and rebirth, but also any threshold or liminal moment.
Pure awareness; the fundamental nature of mind, luminous and empty. The goal of Dzogchen practice.
Emanation body; a recognized reincarnation of a Buddhist master who chooses rebirth to help others.

In the year of the Lord — the Western calendar's epoch, counting from Christ's birth (miscalculated by a few years). Now often replaced by CE (Common Era) to avoid Christian framing while keeping Christian dating.
My fault — acknowledgment of error, formal apology. From Catholic confession. Now secular: the public admission of wrongdoing. Mea maxima culpa: my most grievous fault.

Way of the gods — Japan's indigenous religion of kami worship, purification, and nature reverence. No founder, no scripture, no creed. State Shinto (1868-1945) was different: invented tradition serving nationalism. The original remains.

God, spirit, sacred — the divine beings of Shinto, inhabiting nature, ancestors, and remarkable things. Not creator gods but immanent presences. Eight million kami: rocks, rivers, ancestors, emperors. The sacred is everywhere.
To make something worse by trying to improve it; a well-intentioned 'improvement' that backfires.
terms.etymology: From verschlimmern (worsen) + verbessern (improve)

terms.definition: Aristotle's three modes of persuasion — ethos (credibility), pathos (emotion), logos (logic). The complete rhetorical arsenal. Most persuasion is pathos wearing logos costume, delivered by ethos.
Weight on one leg, the body's axis in S-curve. Greek revolution from stiff frontality.
Archaic Greek standing male nude. Stiff, frontal, smiling.
Archaic Greek standing draped maiden. The female counterpart to kouros.
Made of gold and ivory. Zeus at Olympia, Athena Parthenos—lost wonders.
Bronze casting method: wax model, clay mold, wax melted out, bronze poured in.
The surface color of bronze from age or chemicals. Green verdigris, brown warmth.
Sculpture projecting from a background surface. Bas-relief (low), alto-relief (high).
Low relief: figures barely project from the background.
High relief: figures project boldly, nearly freestanding.
Incised or sunken relief: the image cut into the surface. Opposite of cameo.
A raised relief carved from layered stone, the figure in one color against another.
A small preliminary model for a larger sculpture. The sketch in three dimensions.
The internal framework supporting a sculpture, especially in clay modeling.
A technique for transferring a model's measurements to a marble block.
Subtractive sculpture: removing material to reveal form. Stone, wood.
Additive sculpture: building up form with clay, wax, plaster.
Three-dimensional collage: combining found objects. Picasso, Cornell.
Sculpture that moves. Calder's mobiles, Tinguely's machines.
A hanging kinetic sculpture balanced to move with air currents. Calder's invention.
A stationary abstract sculpture, as opposed to mobile. Also Calder's term.
An ordinary object designated as art. Duchamp's urinal, bicycle wheel.
Art that transforms a space. The viewer enters the work.
Large-scale sculpture using the landscape itself. Smithson's Spiral Jetty.
Art made for a particular location, inseparable from its place.
A sculpture of head, shoulders, and chest. Portrait and presence.
A sculpture of the trunk without head or limbs. Fragmentary beauty.
A sculpture of a rider on horseback. Power and command.
A pillar topped with a head, originally Hermes. Boundary markers, garden ornaments.
The base or pedestal on which a sculpture stands.
Fired clay, unglazed. From Etruscan tombs to Chinese warriors.
Multi-colored: sculpture painted in many colors. Greek statues were polychrome.
Deliberately unfinished: figures emerging from rough stone. Michelangelo's slaves.
Carved or modeled cloth. The Greek 'wet drapery' style clings revealingly.
Perfecting the human form beyond nature. Greek gods in marble.
Faithful representation of natural appearances. Hellenistic old women, Roman portraits.
The fixed smile on early Greek kouroi and korai. Convention, not emotion.
Early Classical Greek sculpture: simplified forms, solemn faces. After the archaic smile.
The peak of Greek sculpture: Phidias, Polykleitos. Ideal beauty achieved.
Greek sculpture after Alexander: emotional, dramatic, virtuosic. Laocoön.
A Hindu sacred image: embodiment of the divine, not mere representation.
Three-bend pose in Indian sculpture: head, torso, hips in opposite directions.
The fear-not gesture: palm outward. Buddhist and Hindu iconography.
Meditation gesture: hands in lap, palms up. The Buddha in contemplation.
The cranial bump atop Buddha's head, representing enlightenment.
The dot or tuft between Buddha's eyebrows, representing wisdom.
Chinese tomb figurines: servants, animals, objects for the afterlife.
The terracotta army of Qin Shi Huang. Thousands of life-size soldiers.
Japanese miniature carved toggles. Ivory, wood, exquisite detail.
Japanese decorative sculpture for display. Not for wearing like netsuke.
A giant Buddha statue. Nara, Kamakura—Japan's colossi.
Japanese tomb figurines of the Kofun period. Terracotta guardians.
Cast brass plaques and heads from the Kingdom of Benin. African metallurgical mastery.
Kongo power figure: wooden sculpture activated by ritual materials. Nails, mirrors, medicine.
Bamana antelope headdress. Agriculture, fertility, mythical being.
Easter Island monolithic human figures. Ancestors watching over the island.
Polynesian carved human figure. First man, ancestor, powerful presence.
Pacific Northwest monumental carving: stacked crests, figures, histories.
Inuit stone landmarks in human form. 'That which acts like a human.'
Giant Olmec basalt heads. Rulers' portraits, helmeted, powerful.
Mesoamerican reclining figure with offering vessel on belly. Toltec, Maya, Aztec.
A group of friends who gather regularly to share life; the essential Greek social unit beyond family.
Reluctance to impose on others; the considerate restraint of not causing trouble or inconvenience to anyone.
Face; social standing and reputation that one must maintain. Losing face is a serious social failure; giving face shows respect.
terms.etymology: Miàn (face, surface) + zi (suffix)
terms.usage: Understanding mianzi is essential for navigating Chinese social and business relationships.

terms.definition: The subtle art of gauging others' moods, reading the room, and responding appropriately. A form of emotional intelligence central to Korean social harmony.
terms.etymology: From 눈 (nun, eye) + 치 (chi, measure, sense)

terms.definition: Head; also one's personal destiny and inner consciousness. Each person's ori chose their fate before birth.
Spirit, breath, wind; the life force and spiritual essence. Similar to prana or pneuma.
The power to make things happen; divine force of life and creation. The authority to create change.
Ascetic practice; spiritual discipline through austerity. The inner fire of self-transformation.
Life force; vital breath that animates all living things. The energy cultivated in yoga and meditation.
Primordial cosmic energy; the divine feminine creative power. Both goddess and force.
Faith combined with devotion and reverence; trust that goes beyond mere belief to heartfelt commitment.
Selfless service; work performed without attachment to results, offered as devotion. Central to Sikh and Hindu traditions.
A holy fool: feigning madness to speak prophetic truth. Protected by tradition.
Serbian family patron saint's day. Each family has one, celebrated annually.
A flexible approach to problem-solving using limited resources in innovative ways; frugal innovation. Making things work against all odds.
terms.etymology: From Hindi/Punjabi, related to 'fixing' or 'work-around'

terms.definition: The lengthwise threads held taut on a loom. The skeleton of the fabric.
The crosswise threads woven through the warp. Also called woof.
The finished edge of fabric that prevents unraveling. Self-edge.
Dyeing technique where threads are tied and dyed before weaving. Blurred, feathered patterns.
Indonesian wax-resist dyeing on fabric. UNESCO heritage. Intricate patterns.
Japanese shaped-resist dyeing: binding, stitching, folding before dyeing.
Weaving with programmed pattern cards. The first computers were looms.
Reversible figured fabric with pattern woven in. Named for Damascus.
Richly decorative fabric with raised patterns, often with gold or silver thread.
Weft-faced weaving creating pictorial or patterned fabric. Gobelin, Bayeux.
Weave with diagonal rib pattern. Denim is a twill.
Weave with floats creating smooth, lustrous surface.
The simplest weave: over one, under one. Also tabby weave.
The roller holding wound warp threads at the back of the loom.
The looped wire or cord through which warp threads pass, controlling the shed.
The opening between raised and lowered warp threads through which the shuttle passes.
The tool carrying the weft thread through the shed.
The frame that pushes each weft thread into place.
Ghanaian strip-woven cloth. Asante royalty. Bright geometric patterns.
Malian cloth dyed with fermented mud. Geometric patterns, natural browns.
Japanese ikat technique. Indigo and white geometric patterns.
Kyoto's luxury silk-weaving district. Obi sashes, brocades.
Fine cashmere wool from Himalayan goats. Kashmiri shawls.
Glazed printed cotton. From Hindi 'chint' (variegated). India to Europe.
Plain-woven cotton, originally from Calicut, India.
Fine cotton fabric from Mosul. So sheer it was called 'woven air.'
Woven fabric with cut pile, creating soft surface. Luxury since Renaissance.
Cotton fabric with vertical ribs (wales). 'Corde du roi'—king's cord.
Scottish plaid pattern: horizontal and vertical bands creating checks. Clan identity.
Two-tone check pattern with jagged edges. Broken checks.
V-shaped twill weave resembling fish skeleton.
Cotton or linen fabric, or the scenic printed 'Toile de Jouy' style.
Thin, stiff, transparent silk or synthetic. Wedding dresses, millinery.
Fine netting, originally silk. Named for Tulle, France. Ballet tutus.
Non-woven fabric: fibers matted together by heat, moisture, pressure. Ancient.
Pacific Island bark cloth. Beaten from paper mulberry. Painted designs.
The art of dramatic composition and theatrical representation. A dramaturg researches, advises on text, and bridges playwright and production.
The final resolution of a plot's complications. From French 'unknotting'—the moment when all threads are untangled.
A speech in which a character speaks their thoughts aloud while alone on stage. The audience becomes privy to the inner mind.
terms.etymology: Latin solus (alone) + loqui (to speak)

terms.definition: A remark spoken to the audience that other characters supposedly cannot hear. A theatrical conspiracy between actor and viewer.
The imaginary barrier between performers and audience. 'Breaking' it means directly acknowledging the audience—shattering the illusion.
The precise staging of actors' movements and positions. Where you stand, when you move—the choreography of drama.
The backstage room where performers wait before going on stage. Origin disputed—possibly from green baize fabric or nervous pallor.
Japanese masked drama: slow, symbolic, austere. Warrior ghosts, possessed women.
Comic interludes between Noh plays. Servants, deception, slapstick.
Flamboyant Japanese theater: elaborate costumes, stylized acting, all-male casts.
Male Kabuki actors specializing in female roles. Idealized femininity.
Kabuki's dramatic pose: crossed eyes, frozen moment. The Instagram of Edo.
Kabuki's runway through the audience. 'Flower path.'
Japanese puppet theater with visible puppeteers. Three operators per puppet.
Kerala dance-drama: green faces, elaborate makeup, all-night performances.
Ancient Sanskrit drama of Kerala. UNESCO heritage. 2000-year tradition.
Karnataka dance-drama: colorful costumes, mythology, improvisation.
Beijing opera: singing, mime, acrobatics, martial arts. Painted faces.
Elegant Chinese opera from Kunshan. UNESCO masterpiece. Refined, lyrical.
Ancient Chinese comic dialogue. Ancestor of xiangsheng.
Javanese puppet theater: flat leather figures behind a screen. All night.
Italian masked improvised comedy. Stock characters: Harlequin, Pantalone, Columbina.
Comic routines in commedia dell'arte. Physical gags, interpolated business.
Servant characters in commedia. The tricksters. Root of 'zany.'
Harlequin: the acrobatic servant in patchwork. Commedia's trickster.
Silent acting with gesture; also British Christmas theatrical tradition.
Comic parody; later, striptease entertainment.
American variety entertainment: songs, comedy, acrobatics. Died with cinema.
Exaggerated drama with music, clear villains and heroes. Now pejorative.
Political propaganda theater. Soviet avant-garde, later global.
Brecht's 'alienation effect': breaking illusion so audiences think critically.
The rear of the stage (originally elevated). To upstage: steal focus.
The front of the stage, nearest the audience.
The sides of the stage, hidden from audience. Where actors wait.
Rigging for raising and lowering scenery and lights.
What the audience can see from their seats. Blocking considers sightlines.
The text of an opera. 'Little book.'
Speech-like singing advancing the plot between arias.
A short, simple aria, often a character's entrance.
The fast, brilliant conclusion to a two-part aria.
A piece for multiple singers. Duet, trio, quartet, finale.
The closing scene of an act, often complex with multiple voices.
Orchestral introduction to an opera, setting mood or previewing themes.
A shorter orchestral opening, leading directly into action. Wagner's term.
Music between acts or scenes. Originally, a comic piece between serious acts.
The highest female voice. Leads, heroines, ingénues.
Middle female voice. Villainesses, mothers, trousers roles.
The lowest female voice. Rare, dark, mysterious.
High male voice. Heroes, lovers, the leading man.
Middle male voice. Fathers, rivals, villains.
The lowest male voice. Kings, priests, devils.
A voice pushed toward dramatic weight. Between lyric and dramatic.
Voice category system in German opera. Your Fach determines your roles.
Hired applauders. A 19th-century opera institution.
'First lady': the lead soprano. Now also: a temperamental star.
A male opera star. Less common than 'diva.'
Realist Italian opera: working-class characters, violent passions. Puccini, Mascagni.
German opera with spoken dialogue. Mozart's Magic Flute.
Light opera with spoken dialogue, dancing. Offenbach, Strauss.
Spanish operetta: spoken and sung, often folk-flavored.
A state where no player benefits from changing strategy alone. Stable but not optimal.
Two players gain most by cooperating, but incentive favors betrayal. The tragedy of rationality.
One player's gain equals another's loss. Total value constant.
Games where total gains can increase. Cooperation possible.
A strategy that's best regardless of what opponents do.
A state where no one can be made better off without making someone worse off.
Minimizing the maximum possible loss. Conservative strategy.
Cooperate first, then mirror opponent's last move. Surprisingly effective.
Two players drive at each other; first to swerve loses face. Brinksmanship.
Cooperation yields the big prize, but solo action is safer. Trust dilemma.
Coordination game: both prefer different options but want to be together.
Schelling point: a solution people gravitate to without communication.
Designing rules so self-interested players achieve desired outcomes. Reverse game theory.
Actions conveying information about private knowledge. Costly signals are credible.
Designing choices that make others reveal their type.
A mechanism that binds you to a future action. Burning bridges.
Solving sequential games by reasoning backward from the end.
A Nash equilibrium that's also Nash in every subgame. No empty threats.
A game with incomplete information. Players have beliefs about others' types.
Everyone knows X, everyone knows everyone knows X, ad infinitum.
Randomizing between pure strategies with specific probabilities.
Equilibrium robust to small probability of mistakes. No hair-trigger instability.
A strategy that, if adopted by a population, cannot be invaded by mutants.
Shared resources depleted because individual incentives diverge from collective good.
Enjoying benefits without contributing. Public goods dilemma.
Expending resources to capture existing wealth rather than create it.
A game where players benefit from making the same choice. Driving on the same side.
Game representation as a tree: nodes are decisions, branches are choices.
Game represented as a payoff matrix. All strategies enumerated.
Study of bidding strategies and auction design. English, Dutch, Vickrey.
In common-value auctions, the winner often overbids. Winning can mean losing.
Proposer offers a split; responder accepts or both get nothing. Tests rationality.
One player simply allocates. No strategic element—tests pure altruism.
Sequential game where pot grows but either player can grab it. Tests backward induction.
The adjustment of space between individual letter pairs to achieve visually pleasing spacing. Poor kerning creates awkward gaps or collisions.
The vertical space between lines of text, measured from baseline to baseline. Named for the thin strips of lead placed between lines of metal type.
terms.etymology: From lead strips in letterpress

terms.definition: Two or more letters combined into a single glyph, such as fi, fl, or æ. Originally a practical solution to letters that collided in metal type.
A statement at the end of a book giving details of its production—printer, typeface, paper. From ancient Greek practice of noting the scribe's name.
terms.etymology: Greek kolophōn (summit, finishing touch)

terms.definition: Books printed before 1501, during the infancy of printing. The term evokes swaddling clothes—these are books from when print was in its cradle.
terms.etymology: Latin incunabula (swaddling clothes, cradle)

terms.definition: Recto: the front (right-hand) page of a book. Verso: the back (left-hand) page. From the Latin for 'right' and 'turned'.
The inner margin of a book page, near the binding. Must be wide enough for comfortable reading without cracking the spine.
A widow is a lone line at the top of a page. An orphan is a lone line at the bottom. Both are considered typographic sins—no line should be left alone.
The part of a lowercase letter extending above the x-height: b, d, f, h, k, l. Reaching upward.
The part of a lowercase letter extending below the baseline: g, j, p, q, y. Reaching downward.
The height of lowercase letters without ascenders or descenders—measured by 'x'. Determines a typeface's apparent size.
The invisible line on which letters sit. Most characters rest here; descenders drop below it.
The small projecting feature at the end of letter strokes. Times New Roman has serifs; Helvetica doesn't.
A typeface without serifs—clean, modern, geometric. 'Sans' is French for 'without'.
The enclosed or partially enclosed space within a letter: the hole in 'o', the bowl of 'a'.
The curved part of a letter enclosing a counter: the round part of 'b', 'd', 'p', 'o'.
The main vertical stroke of a letter. The backbone of 'l', the uprights of 'H'.
A horizontal stroke connecting two stems, as in 'H' and 'A'. Also called a bar.
The tapered or curved end of a stroke that doesn't terminate in a serif. The elegant finishing touch.
An ornamental extension or flourish on a letter. Decorative swashes add calligraphic flair to type.
The end of a stroke that doesn't have a serif. Ball terminals are rounded; beak terminals are pointed.
The point where two strokes meet at the top of a letter, as in 'A'. The typographic peak.
The point where two strokes meet at the bottom of a letter, as in 'V'. The typographic valley.
The interior angle where two strokes meet, as inside the 'V'. The apex seen from inside.
The curved stroke of 'h', 'm', 'n' connecting the stem to the arch.
The main curved stroke of 'S'. The letter's sinuous backbone.
A small projection from a main stroke, smaller than a serif. An accent of attitude.
The descending stroke of 'Q', 'R', or 'K'. The letter's signature flourish.
The small stroke projecting from the top of lowercase 'g'. Not all g's have ears.
The stroke connecting the two bowls of a double-story 'g'.
The lower bowl of a double-story 'g'. Some typefaces have open loops; others closed.
The downward diagonal stroke of 'K', 'R', and 'k'. Not quite a tail, not quite a stem.
A horizontal stroke that doesn't connect on one or both ends: the top of 'T', the strokes of 'E'.
The uniform adjustment of space between all characters in a block of text. Looser or tighter overall.
A unit equal to the current point size. An em-dash is one em wide. Named for the width of 'M' in metal type.
Half an em. An en-dash is used for ranges (1990–2000). Named for the width of 'N'.
A unit of type measurement equal to 12 points, or about 1/6 inch. The inch of typography.
The smallest unit of type measurement—approximately 1/72 inch. 12 points make a pica.
A page number, or a sheet folded once to make two leaves (four pages). From Latin 'leaf'.
A left-hand page in a book (even-numbered). The back of a leaf. Opposite of recto.
A right-hand page in a book (odd-numbered). The front of a leaf. Where chapters traditionally begin.
A folded sheet forming a section of a book, typically 8, 16, or 32 pages. Books are bound signature by signature.
The arrangement of pages on a press sheet so they'll be in order when folded. The printer's spatial puzzle.
When a printed element extends beyond the trim edge. The image 'bleeds' off the page—no white margin.
The final cut size of a printed piece. What remains after the edges are cut away.
In hot metal, a line of type cast as a single piece. Also the space for running headers/footers.
The width of a column of text, usually in picas. Ideal measure: 45-75 characters for comfortable reading.
The uneven edge of a column of text set flush left or right. A good rag has gentle, not jagged, undulation.
Distracting vertical gaps in text caused by word spaces aligning across multiple lines. A sign of bad justification.
A single word or short line at the end of a paragraph. Left behind, looking lonely.
Setting punctuation slightly outside the text margin for optical alignment. The margin looks straighter.
Capital letters drawn at roughly x-height. Used for acronyms, abbreviations, and elegant headers.
Numerals with varying heights—some ascending, some descending—that blend with lowercase text. Also called text figures.
Numerals of uniform height, aligning with capitals. Modern and tabular, but can look clunky in running text.
An ornamental character or symbol—bullets, stars, pointing hands. The typographer's garnish.
A typographic ornament resembling a flower or leaf. Used to decorate or separate text. The printer's flower.
The paragraph symbol: ¶. From Greek 'paragraphos'. Once marked new paragraphs before indentation became standard.
A pointing hand symbol: ☞. Used in margins to draw attention. From Latin 'little hand'. Also called a fist.
The first word of the next page printed at the bottom of the current page. Helped binders order loose sheets.
Text printed in red, especially headings or initial letters. From Latin 'ruber' (red). Now means any set of instructions.
The metal frame that holds type and blocks for letterpress printing. The forme goes in the chase.
The assembled type and blocks locked in a chase, ready for printing. What goes on the press.
Expandable wedges that lock type in the chase. Pronounced 'coin'. The pressure that holds it all together.
Blocks of wood or metal used to fill blank spaces in a forme. What isn't type is furniture.
A thin strip of wood used for spacing in letterpress. Smaller than furniture, larger than leading.
Individual pieces of type. To be 'out of sorts' meant lacking specific characters—hence the modern idiom for feeling unwell.
A hand-held adjustable tray for assembling type character by character. The compositor's instrument.
A drawer with compartments for storing type. Capital letters were in the upper case; small letters in the lower case.
A Roman military standard—a cloth square hung from a crossbar. The ancestor of modern flags. Gives vexillology its name.
The upper corner of a flag, typically the hoist side. The U.S. stars occupy the canton.
The half of the flag farthest from the pole—the part that flies free. Also the flag's horizontal length.
The half of the flag nearest the pole. Also the flag's vertical width. You hoist a flag up the pole.
The background color or pattern of a flag. The French field is three vertical stripes; Japan's is white.
Any emblem or device on a flag. Stars, crescents, eagles, symbols—all are charges.
A narrow border separating two colors that would otherwise touch improperly. The white stripes in the Union Jack are fimbriations.
A flag of three horizontal or vertical stripes. France, Germany, Italy, Russia—tribands dominate world flags.
A three-colored flag, specifically vertical stripes. The French tricolore sparked a revolution in flag design.
A two-colored flag divided horizontally or vertically. Poland, Monaco, Ukraine.
An off-center cross extending to the flag's edges, shifted toward the hoist. Denmark, Sweden, Norway, Finland, Iceland.
A zigzag or triangular edge between flag sections. Bahrain's and Qatar's flags have serrated divisions.
A flag with a V-shaped cut in the fly, creating two points. Common in Scandinavian naval ensigns.
A triangular or swallowtail flag, typically identifying a yacht club. A sailor's affiliation.
A small flag carried by military units, often swallow-tailed. The unit's identity in battle.
A long, narrow, tapering flag. Naval signal flags are often pennants.
A banner hung from a crossbar, often with streamers. Medieval Italian city-states carried gonfalons.
A flag indicating nationality, especially flown by ships. The Red, White, and Blue Ensigns of Britain.
A small flag flown at the bow of a warship. The Union Jack is Britain's naval jack.
A flag with the arms or badge of a sovereign or noble. Also a ceremonial or military flag.
A square or vertical flag bearing arms or emblems. Heraldic banners show the full coat of arms.
A national flag for use by civilians. Some nations have different civil and state flags.
A national flag for government use, sometimes with additional emblems. Austria's state flag adds an eagle.
A variant flown by the military or in time of war. Often more elaborate than the civil flag.
A foreign nation's flag flown by a visiting ship as a sign of respect. Maritime diplomacy.
A flag flown below the peak of the pole as a sign of mourning. Leaving room for the invisible flag of death.
To lower a flag briefly as a salute to another ship or dignitary. The U.S. flag is never dipped.
A distinctive part of a flag symbolizing unity—often in the canton. The stars in the U.S. flag form the union.
The material from which flags are made, or festive decorations of flag-like strips. Dressed overall in bunting.
